subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when one addresses the house for the first time in the course of a debate such as this, it is somewhat customary, I believe, to say a few words about one's own constituency. I therefore would like, at the outset, to recall certain political memories concerning the county of Dorchester and the men who have represented it here in this house.
I would like, in particular, Mr. Speaker, to remind you that in 1916 the member for Dorchester was holding the office you are performing today with such dignity. I refer to the Hon. Albert Sevigny who presided over these debates also with great dignity. The Hon. Mr. Sevigny later became a minister in the Borden cabinet, and, had it not been for certain circumstances which are of little interest today, would still be, I believe, the member for Dorchester. Mr. Sevigny is now chief justice of the Superior Court of the province of Quebec over which he presides with the dignity and legal experience which are so well known to all.
The Hon. Lucien Cannon, who was the uncle of the present representative of the Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Cannon), then represented the constituency of Dorchester for about 12 years. He was solicitor general in the Mackenzie King administration. Nobody has forgotten what an able speaker this former member for Dorchester was. I must admit, for my part, that this speaking ability was, to me, a source of the greatest enjoyment when I was still a young man. Later on, the Hon. Mr. Cannon was appointed to the Quebec superior court. His untimely death was a great loss to the bench, among whose most enlightened members he was.
Dorchester also had the privilege of being represented here by one of its native sons, the Hon. Onesime Gagnon, who was a minister in the Bennett cabinet and who is now provincial minister of finance in Quebec. He administers this important department with the same competence, devotion to work and selflessness that he had shown when he sat here.
The Budget-Mr. Perron
And what can we say of my immediate predecessor, the Hon. Leonard Tremblay, who now sits in the Senate, but who represented Dorchester for 18 years. It is always a difficult and delicate thing in circumstances such as these, especially when dealing with political opponents, to speak on topical matters, before the passage of time has completely eliminated all friction. So I shall say about Senator Tremblay, to parody a famous statement: "He did me too much wrong for me to speak well of him, but he did too much good for me to speak ill of him." However I should like to congratulate the government on having appointed him a senator, for he had served his party well and that will enable him to keep on living in the political atmosphere which has always been so dear to him.
Mr. Speaker, need I add that, as a rule, the member for Dorchester is elected with a small majority and that the present member was no exception to the general rule at the last elections. May I say, also, that Dorchester is on the opposition side for the first time. Here, I must confess that it was the other Quebec ridings that were at fault.
Mr. Speaker, I want to deal with two questions of special importance for the province of Quebec, but which have repercussions throughout Canada.
In the first place, I wish to speak to the resolution submitted by the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) amending the Income Tax Act with regard to mutual insurance companies other than mutual life companies.
(Text):

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Order. I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but the constant buzzing that I hear here is most annoying. I cannot hear the hon. member who is speaking; there is too much competition with his voice.
(Translation):

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Secondly, I want to discuss federal-provincial relations, particularly as far as the provincial tax just introduced by the government of Quebec is concerned.
Mr. Speaker, resolution No. 6 of the budget speech, which relates to the taxation of mutual insurance companies and appears on page 3736 of Hansard of April 6, 1954, reads as follows:
Resolved that it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Income Tax Act and to provide, amongst other things:
6.	For the taxation of a resident mutual insurance corporation, other than a life insurance corporation, as though the surplus arising from its insurance activities on and after January 1, 1954 were a profit from a business, and declaring that a

The Budget-Mr. Perron non-resident mutual insurance corporation, other than a life insurance corporation, shall be deemed to be and always to have been subject to taxation on that basis.
Thus the government has decided to tax the income of mutual insurance companies, including mutual fire insurance companies. The government has resolved to put an end to a struggle that has been going on for many years and in which it has never come out on top. In fact, following an investigation by a commission appointed by the government to determine whether co-operatives should be taxable, the commission came to the conclusion that some mutual fire insurance companies should not be taxed. Later on, the Supreme Court of Canada gave a decision along the same line. And these conclusions are quite logical.
The one aim of many mutual fire insurance companies is to help their members in the event of some disaster. They sprang from a charitable purpose. At first, when a farmer lost his farm buildings or his house by fire, the parishioners organized a subscription to compensate him for his loss. Then, it was found more practical and easier to create a relief fund based on yearly contributions. This fund was used to compensate the victims of disasters. In this way there was less delay. There is no question of profits. Those who look after the administration and development of these mutual fire insurance companies give their time voluntarily or almost free of charge and their zeal should not be taxed. There are no dividends, as all profits are turned back into the relief fund. Moreover, it is recognized in the amendment that it cannot be considered as commercial operations or profits, since the law says that the revenue is taxable "as though it were a profit from a business". It is thus recognized that no profits are involved. Moreover, the government commission and the Supreme Court held these same views since they stated in their conclusions that these are co-operatives without capital stock, without dividends, without refunds, and which have been established for the sole purpose of helping their members.
Mr. Speaker, this amendment, in my opinion, is a denial of justice because it is retroactive and makes subject to taxation organizations which, the Supreme Court has ruled, should not be taxed. If, in a given year, there is no fire, the treasury will have the same devastating effect as fire on the finances of these mutual companies.
I am therefore asking the minister to modify this amendment which affects at least


300 mutual fire insurance companies operating in the rural parishes of Quebec and which has created quite a commotion among their 60,000 members. This tax affects the very existence of these mutual companies which are necessary institutions and whose value is beyond doubt. I therefore ask the government to abide by the decisions of the Supreme Court and of the royal commission.
Mr. Speaker, may I be permitted now to broach a question of current interest, which concerns the right of the taxpayers from Quebec to demand that the federal government deduct from their federal income tax the amount which they are called upon to pay under the provincial income tax act. It is a hot issue in that province at the present time, especially since the Minister of Finance rejected the Quebec taxpayers' request.
It is only in this house that there seems to be any argument about the question. In the province concerned, all the people, regardless of political affiliation, unanimously recognize the fact that the federal government has absolutely no grounds to refuse a deduction based upon the most elementary justice.
All the newspapers, French or English, even those which, usually, support the Liberal party, have declared that the federal government was under the obligation to grant such a deduction and for my part I have seen no article in any paper, whatever its political colour or creed, defending the stand taken by the Minister of Finance.
Municipalities, chambers of commerce, labour unions, and a great many public organizations, associations or corporations have made representations and been unanimous in asking for such a deduction.
Opinion has never been so unanimous throughout the province. It is perfectly synchronized; the only false notes have come from the supporters of the government representing Quebec constituencies.
I admit that I find this rather strange and difficult to understand. However, we must recognize that the arguments advanced until now lacked the firmness and conviction usually shown on the other side of the house. Those arguments do not seem to have converted many people in the province of Quebec. Those arguments smell of oil, as Boileau would put it, and in reading them or listening to them one has the impression that they are the result of long sleepless nights.
Mr. Speaker, everything has been said on this matter during the past two months and

In saying that, I do not think that they endangered national unity. Let me quote what Sir Wilfrid Laurier said:
It is a completely false principle which permits one government to receive revenues and another to spend the money; that will always lead to wastefulness.
People have not been up in arms as a result of that statement, so far as I know. On the contrary, I believe everyone applauded it. Today, it is exactly the same thing as we must decide whether the province of Quebec shall or shall not rely on subsidies. In my opinion, we should not worry about national unity, even if some hon. members seem to worry about the Union Nationale.
Quebec has always generously contributed to the assistance given less privileged provinces. She has done so since 1945 without demanding any compensation, while other provinces have received subsidies; Quebec has thereby contributed more than any other province of our confederation to the maintenance of Canada's economic stability. It is not because Quebec wants to avail herself of a right that this economic equilibrium will be disrupted. The people of Quebec understand that they are citizens of a great country and they want to keep on contributing to its development and greatness. In return, they have the right to demand firmly what is rightly theirs. It would only be an act of distributive justice to accede to their request.
Before concluding my remarks, I wish to say that I am proud of my party's stand on this matter. In demanding that we respect the pact which brought about confederation, the Conservative party follows the tradition of its great leaders, Sir George Etienne Cartier and Sir John Macdonald. I am all the more happy at the stand taken by my party that it was the very stand taken by such great Liberal leaders as Laurier, Mackenzie King, Taschereau, Lapointe, and others, during more than half a century. The Liberal party is shunning its past in favour of a centralization which is the very negation of the principle embodied in the constitution, and such centralization is bound to have evil consequences on Canadian politics. Fortunately, we are in a position to foresee that the Conservative party, which was responsible for confederation, will be one day entrusted by the Canadian people with the task of stemming the tide of centralization and of rebuilding that which will have been destroyed.
Because of the importance of this question of personal income tax, and because this government has turned down the Quebec

taxpayers' request, I take the liberty, Mr. Speaker, before resuming my seat, of appealing from this decision to the Prime Minister himself. I do so on behalf of 300,000 taxpayers and in the very name of justice, placing this question outside and above the realm of political partisanship.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. Ross Thatcher (Moose Jaw-Lake Centre):
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words on this legislation before it is passed. I assume that this will be the last budget the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) will bring down. I hope to spend about 30 minutes telling him what I do not like about his current effort. Nevertheless, I think I should say in passing that I am sure history will record that the Minister of Finance has done a first-class job in the years during which he has been Minister of Finance.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in analysing this current budget, one fact very quickly emerges. Nine years after the war, at a time when most Canadians are tired and weary of heavy federal taxation, the government once again is providing little or no tax relief. The concessions offered by the minister in his speech before Easter amounted only to about $40 million. If we work that amount out on a per capita basis, it means that the average Canadian this year will receive tax relief of only about $2.67 each. Surely hon. members will admit that this reduction is trifling and insignificant.
During the coming year the minister is proposing to take the staggering sum of $4,460 million from the pockets of the Canadian people. I believe this total is about $60 million more than he took from them last year. I am convinced, Mr. Speaker, that our present tax burden is already adversely affecting the Canadian economy, particularly in the fields of employment and trade. In the first place, of course, it is obvious that high taxes blunt incentive and discourage initiative. Today it is also obvious that federal taxation is lowering consumer purchasing power in the domestic market. Very substantial sums which the average Canadian might otherwise spend to build a house, buy an automobile, or purchase farm machinery, are being siphoned off in high taxes. The resulting reduction in the demand for goods is reflected in many Canadian cities today in reduced demand for labour.
In the third place, I think that even the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) would have to admit that our present tax level is hurting our investment program in new plant and new equipment. I think we would have been in trouble several years ago had it not
The Budget-Mr. Thatcher been for the heavy influx of United States capital. Personally I have always believed -and I believe today-that, where taxation is concerned, there is a point of diminishing returns. When that point has been exceeded, individual and corporate saving is hindered, and the creation of new jobs is jeopardized.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I contend that our present tax rate in Canada is helping to force up the Canadian cost structure. Many authorities tell us that Canadian prices are among the highest in the world. We are being undersold in both the domestic and the export market in many instances. We are being undersold despite our modern factories, despite our proximity to natural resources, and despite our technical knowledge. I contend that one of the reasons we are being undersold, is the heavy federal tax burden which is imposed upon Canadian producers. During the past winter Canada experienced a mild but very definite economic recession. At one time we had more than 540,000 persons unemployed. That was a greater number unemployed than Great Britain had in the same period. In proportion to population, I think it was a greater number of unemployed than the United States had. Yet, in this budget, the government has taken virtually no steps to deal with the problem of unemployment.
I believe that the primary aim of this budget should be to check the present mild recession in Canada before it becomes really serious. The government should adopt fiscal policies which would make the economic climate more favourable for individuals and for business to expand, thus indirectly creating a greater demand for labour. As I see it, the first step in promoting such expansion should be a sharp reduction in federal taxation. The minister argues that if he cut taxes, he would lose revenue that he needs. In taking such a position it seems to me that he is failing to grapple with the basic problem involved. I contend that he could reduce taxation yet still balance his budget, if he would curtail relatively unnecessary expenditures, and if he would eliminate waste, extravagance and duplication in government services. Surely a dollar saved by economy means just as much to the federal treasury as does a dollar collected in taxes.
In his budget speech the minister admonished Canadian industry to eliminate waste and to cut expenses. I think that Canadian business would take that advice more to heart, Mr. Speaker, if the minister and his colleagues had themselves been setting a better example in conducting the biggest business in the country, which is the federal

The Budget-Mr. Thatcher government. In his speech before Easter the minister gave no assurance whatever to the people of Canada that he planned to be more thrifty. Not a word was spoken, nor a promise given, concerning the elimination of waste or the reduction of costs in government. I remind the Minister of Finance of the old adage, that actions speak louder than words. I think his advice would be more effective if he practised what he preached. In his budget speech of a year ago about the main contribution he made with regard to saving was this, and I quote from page 2121 of Hansard of 1953:
We are, for example, this year inaugurating a suggestion awards plan in the civil service which we are confident will, over the course of time, result in many major and minor improvements in efficiency of operation . . .
What saving has the plan produced? I quote from Hansard of December 9, 1953 at page 735:
Approximately 30 suggestions have been implemented which will result in an estimated savings of $6,500 for the first year each actual suggestion in efficiency of operation . . .
I think savings of that kind are rather paltry. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that in this house the word "economy" is like a foreign language. If you mention it too often, you are likely to get into trouble. Yet if we are going to have real tax reductions in the near future I think something must be done to cut federal expenditures.
Time and again the Minister of Finance has suggested to opposition members that they should be specific, and that they should try to pinpoint places where they think savings could be made. I have gone over the estimates this year, as I have gone over them in the past. I shall try to make specific suggestions again this afternoon, even though I know many hon. members may not agree with what I have to say. I should like to make a few proposals to the minister for his consideration.
My first specific suggestion has to do with the Canadian National Railways. According to a report which was recently carried by the Montreal Star and other papers, the C.N.R. is proposing this year to build a 1,000-room hotel in the city of Montreal. The new building is to be a luxury hotel which will accommodate 2,500 people at banquets and 4,000 people at conventions. The president of the C.N.R, is not proposing to build this hotel out of revenue. Rather he is coming once again to the taxpayers of Canada for another handout. I suggest that there are certain reasons why this handout should not be forthcoming.
Two years ago parliament approved a reorganization of the capital stock of the


C.N.R. That reorganization had the net effect of wiping out approximately $1 billion in liabilities and substituted therefor noninterest bearing stock. At that time we were given the assurance that, if the reorganization went through, the profit and loss picture of the C.N.R. would be greatly improved. To a degree it has improved. Nevertheless, despite the reorganization, and despite the fact that the C.N.R. has literally billions of dollars invested, in 1952 it was able to show a profit of only $142,000 and in 1953 of only $244,000. A few weeks ago, when appearing before a parliamentary committee, President Gordon told that committee that he expected the railroad this year would once again be deeply in the red.
Perhaps I do not know very much about business, but it seems to me that it is not sound business practice for a company to indulge in luxury expenditures at a time when it has a substantial deficit. I think this should be particularly true with regard to the C.N.R., when we look at the past record of their hotel system. The profit and loss picture of the hotel system has never been particularly good. One of the best years was 1952. In that year, with an investment of $31-5 million, the hotel system showed a profit of $535,000. But even that profit was only a bookkeeping profit, as the annual statement points out, because adequate depreciation reserves were not set up. Yet despite the past history of the hotel system, Mr. Gordon now comes before parliament and suggests that the taxpayers should spend another $20 million on another hotel. How are we to know that this building might not be another white elephant? I want to tell the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) that in my opinion the people of Canada are most willing to finance capital expenditures for the C.N.R. if or when they are opening up and developing the country. Such a policy is sensible and logical in a country like Canada. But I do not believe that the building of a luxury hotel any place in Canada falls within that category of expenditure. When Mr. Gordon can show a substantial profit for the C.N.R. let him come to parliament and propose to spend that profit any way he wishes. If he wants to build a hotel, that will be his business; but until the time comes when he can build it out of revenue it seems to me that such an expenditure should be struck from the estimates.

What is the difference? The C.N.R. is owned by the government. I would refer the house next to item 179 of the estimates of the Department of Labour. This item proposes the expenditure of just under $1 million for the administration of the annuities act. In addition to the amount for administrative costs, a sum of $1 million is also being sought in order to keep the fund on a sound actuarial basis. The original purpose of the annuities act was to permit people of moderate means to make provision for their old age. Even with the advent of a better old age pension scheme I think there is a place for the annuities act in our overall system of social security. On the other hand, I cannot convince myself-and I am speaking only for myself-that it is sound or sensible to sell federal government annuities at less than cost.
Since the inception of this legislation the taxpayers have been forced to bear costs in the neighbourhood of $33 million. I strongly believe that when government annuities are sold, the premiums should be sufficient (1) to carry the administrative costs and (2) to keep the fund sound. I think that annuities could still be sold at prices which would be most competitive and considerably under the prices that insurance companies charge for similar kinds of policies. I emphasize that I think the annuities act is a useful piece of legislation, but I urge the government to save roughly $2 million annually by making operations under the act self-sustaining.

speechtext: Before my hon. friend goes on to something else, may I be permitted to ask a question? May I ask if his remarks regarding annuities represent the present policy of his party?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I thought I made that very clear. I said that I was speaking personally. I am quite sure that the leader of this group and probably certain others do not feel as I do, but I still think it is a matter which, as a member of parliament, I should discuss. I trust I have made myself clear.
Item 98 in the estimates of the Department of External Affairs calls for an expenditure of $200,000 for the international civil aviation organization. The purpose of the vote
The Budget-Mr. Thatcher is to provide the organization with rental charges at less than commercial rates. When the vote was originally authorized in 1950 the amount was only $64,000, but the amount has been increasing each year. Up to the start of the present fiscal year the taxpayers have subsidized the organization to a total of $310,000. May I say at once that I think Canadians are most happy to have the headquarters of the organization in Canada but, speaking for myself, I can see no reason why the organization, like Canadian organizations, should not pay its own rent. I believe that the subsidy of $200,000 should be discontinued.
I draw the attention of the house to items 53 and 54 of the estimates which call for the expenditure of approximately $2,400,000 for the overseas shortwave broadcasting service. I remind the house that this service was originally inaugurated during the war, and my understanding is, that its main purpose was to keep in contact with our troops overseas. When our troops came home, there was of course no need for this type of communication. It is quite true that the broadcasts have some propaganda value overseas but I do not think that the costs, which have been increasing year by year, are anywhere in line with the value received by the Canadian taxpayer. The elimination of this expenditure could save the taxpayer $2,400,000.
In the fifth place, I think that a good deal of money could be saved by the elimination of duplication in various government departments. I believe, rightly or wrongly, that since coming to Ottawa I have seen overlapping which no business firm could afford. I should like to give the house an example of what I have in mind. I would refer hon. members to sessional paper 161-A. That return shows that in the city of Ottawa alone, the federal government today maintains forty-five separate and distinct libraries, at a total cost to the taxpayers of $750,000. The Department of Justice has three separate libraries. The Department of Mines and Technical Surveys has four separate libraries. The Department of National Defence has seven separate libraries in the Ottawa area alone. The Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources maintains five separate libraries. The Department of the Secretary of State contains two, the Department of National Revenue has two, and so on.
In addition to the libraries operated by the different government departments, there are those in such agencies as the national film board, the civil service commission, the public archives, the R.C.M.P., Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and so on. I simply cannot believe that so many libraries do not represent duplication. I

The Budget-Mr. Thatcher suggest to the Minister of Finance that if he would consolidate them he could probably save in the neighbourhood of $250,000. I suggest also that the example of libraries is only typical. It seems to me that the government is riddled with similar types of duplication in government departments.
I should like to refer now to sessional paper 120-B which was tabled for me earlier this session. This sessional paper shows that in the past year, the atomic energy control board made two grants at Deep River for the building of churches. The first grant was for $75,000 and was made to St. Alexander's parish church, a Roman Catholic church. The second grant of $142,000 was made to the community church, a Protestant church. Both churches were fairly elaborate in their construction. I should like to quote from the Ottawa valley Ensign of November 21, 1953, which contains a report of the proceedings at the laying of the cornerstone of the Roman Catholic church. The paragraph reads as follows:
The future church, an apricot brick structure, will feature tinted glass windows, a bell tower displaying a 60-foot high spire, laminated wood trusses of Gothic design in the interior, and a baptistry directly below the bell tower.
In other words, it is a fairly luxurious church, and obviously the Protestant church is even more so because almost double the amount of money has been spent on it. I take exception to these grants for two main reasons. In the first place, as far as I can find-and I am subject to correction if I am wrong-these items were not in the estimates. If they were, they were certainly well hidden, and I do not think parliament discussed the expenditures before they were made. In the second place, I object to expenditures of this kind because in my constituency, and I think in other constituencies in Canada, the people themselves contribute towards the building of churches. It seems to me that this expenditure singles out one separate community for special treatment. I do not think it is fair that people elsewhere in Canada should have to contribute taxes to build a church in any community, and I hope that expenditures of this nature will not happen again.
Item 76 in the estimates proposes to provide $130,000 for a number of paintings for the national gallery. This is in addition to the expenditure of $350,000 made late in March for that same purpose. Personally, I cannot become too enthused about expenditures of this kind. It seems to me that in this period of heavy federal taxation some kind of limit should be put on them. I suggest that, at the very outside, the national gallery should spend in any one year no


more than $150,000. If that had been done this year the taxpayers could have been saved $330,000.
In the seventh place, I think one of the very foolish expenditures, if I may call it that, was connected with the government's decision this year to move the film board down to the city of Montreal. My understanding is that by the time that palatial home is completed, and by the time a staff of 475 and their families are transferred, the taxpayers will be out between $6 million and $7 million. I guess it is too late to do anything about it; but if it were possible I would certainly suggest to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) that he could save that $7 million very easily by leaving the board in Ottawa, without the service being impaired.
In the eighth place, I feel impelled to say a few words about the civil service. And I want to emphasize, as I did when the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) queried me, that I am only speaking personally, and not for this group. However, as elected representatives I think it is our duty from time to time to go over the payroll of the civil service. Now, it is a fact that in recent years our civil service numbers have been increasing very rapidly. I would remind the house that at the outbreak of war in 1939, Canada had a civil service that, in all, totalled 46,106 persons. During the height of the war, when we had such organizations as the wartime prices and trade board, rationing boards and the like, our civil service was only 115,000 persons. By 1950 it had moved up to 125,000; and according to a parliamentary return, at the beginning of this year our civil service numbered 135,000. If you add casual employees, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, commission employees, and ships' crews to our civil service, then at the start of the year it numbered 172,000. And that figure still did not include the 152,000 who were employed in government corporations and agencies.
Now, it is quite true that Canada has grown mightily in wealth and in resources since 1939. But I find it rather hard to understand why, with a population increase of 40 per cent since 1939, our civil service should have almost tripled in number. I think our record in this regard should be examined all the more carefully when we compare what 'has been happening in Canada with what has been happening in the United States and Great Britain. From October 1952 to October 1953 in the United States, under the Eisenhower administration, the civil service was reduced by 197,000 employees or 10 per cent.

Last year Prime Minister Churchill was able to reduce the civil service in Great Britain by 20,000.
Now, in view of those figures many taxpayers throughout Canada are wondering if it is really necessary for our civil service to continue to grow and grow. Today in Ottawa scarcely a week goes by when some new board or commission is not set up. And when a new office is set up it must have a new staff. My experience has been-and I am speaking generally-that when a board is disbanded, usually the employees who were working for it are simply sent over to some other branch of the civil service. Over the years, that kind of policy cannot help but tend to impair efficiency.
I am speaking subject to correction, of course, but as I see this problem there are some departments which have superfluous civil servants. I shall give one specific example to the Minister of Finance, in the hope that he might examine it. This has to do with the office of the deputy minister of national defence. In 1944, at the height of the war, the combined offices of the deputy ministers of air, army and navy had a staff of 98. In 1946 there were only 77. But today, according to a parliamentary return tabled earlier in the house, Mr. Drury's office has 114. There may be a reason for the expansion; but on the surface, at least, it looks to me as though there might 'be something out of line. I feel that the number of government employees could be reduced without impairing efficiency. I am not suggesting that the government should commence any large-scale program of dismissals. I know that such a program would not be feasible, nor would it be desirable. But I do suggest that, generally speaking, the numbers of the civil service should be frozen at the present level, even though a few exceptions might have to be made. I think a sharp reduction could be accomplished if vacancies in the future were not filled by new appointments, but rather were filled by a reshuffling of existing personnel. If treasury board should see fit to indulge in such an economy drive, I believe the taxpayers of Canada in the coming year could save $30 million or $40 million.
My ninth suggestion has to do with item 283 of the estimates, and the subject of national fitness, which comes under the Department of National Health and Welfare. I I am pleased to see that there is an expenditure this year of only $78,000. This expenditure has been reduced by about $125,000 annually over the last several years. But I still do not think we have done quite well enough. When this legislation was inaugurated during the
The Budget-Mr. Thatcher war, it was for the purpose of co-ordinating physical fitness programs among the various provinces. Actually, while it has done a certain amount of good in distributing literature, and the like, by and large the program has been a disappointment. In the first place, two provinces did not come into it at all; and in the second place the division which was supposed to be interested chiefly in physical education has, in later years, become mainly interested in adult education, including such things as the drama. I do not think the taxpayers are getting value for their money and I suggest the item should be deleted from the estimates.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Perhaps you and I are in agreement.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

I hope so, Mr. Minister.
I refer next to the estimates of the Post Office Department. Hon. members will recall that early last year the department had the firm of J. D. Woods and Gordon Limited come in to do an examination to see whether greater efficiency was possible. One of the major recommendations of the company was that the post office savings branch should be discontinued. Company officials claimed a saving of $377,000 could be made. I am aware of the reasons given by the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote) as to why he did not think this was a logical saving. Nevertheless I would like to see the matter re-examined. I think there was merit in the Woods and Gordon suggestion.
In the eleventh place I would refer to item 251 in the estimates, which has to do with sick mariners' treatment service. Since confederation the treatment of sick mariners on a prepaid basis has been provided at Canadian ports. Under the Canada Shipping Act tonnage duties are levied against ships using this service to offset the cost of providing the treatment.
In the year 1952-53, according to the public accounts, 20,000 Canadians were treated under the provisions of the act and 89,000 foreign seamen. That year the cost of the service to the taxpayer was $588,000. Yet, the revenue collected on duties was only $340,000, or a net loss of about $250,000. Perhaps there are reasons why my suggestion would not be feasible, but it seems to me that it would be logical to increase the duties which are charged for this service until they cover the cost. If that could be done I suggest that the taxpayer could be saved in the neighbourhood of $250,000 a year.

A saving which I mentioned a year ago had to do with the printing of government pamphlets, bulletins and publications, which seem to me to be of little value to the taxpayers. It is headed: "Canadian Government Publications." As one looks through the publication, he cannot help but be appalled at some of the things on which the government is spending money to have printed. I recall the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace (Mr. Hamilton) pointing out some of these pamphlets. For instance, on page 213 I find one having to do with the "Cruising speed of goldfish in relation to water temperature". subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will do that if the minister will do one thing for me. If he or the Minister of Finance will have the queen's printer assemble in the railway committee room every pamphlet, bulletin, etc., published by the government in the past year, for examination by members, I will accept his suggestion. If he did that, even he and the Minister of Finance would be surprised at the waste.
I still contend that the taxpayers could be saved several millions of dollars if some of these unnecessary pamphlets and bulletins were not printed.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I regret that the government still has not seen fit to set up a central purchasing agency to purchase supplies and materials for the crown. Today there are dozens of different branches that are making purchases for the crown. Sometimes these branches are actually competing against each other. I doubt whether there is a single large company in the Dominion of Canada which has not a central purchasing department. Out in the province of Saskatchewan we tried it some years ago, and the provincial minister tells me that he has been able to effect a good many economies through bulk buying. A central purchasing agency of the federal government could effect very substantial economies by taking advantage of maximum quantity discounts through bulk buying. I can only guess, but I would estimate that about $10 million could be saved in a year if the minister wanted to carry out this suggestion.
I know that I have only touched on the problem of saving very superficially. Nevertheless at least it gives some indication of what I have in mind, and I suggest that if

some of the economies which I have mentioned today were put into effect a minimum of $75 million could be saved. At the same time, I also realize that if we are to make major economies it will have to come from the Department of National Defence.
I am not going into the Department of National Defence in detail but events have transpired in the last year which make me wonder whether it would not be possible to have modest defence cuts. In the first place, the shooting war in Korea has ended; and it would seem that the international situation has bettered somewhat. During the past year President Eisenhower, who is perhaps one of the greatest military men living, has seen fit to ask the United States government to carry out cuts of 10 per cent in defence expenditures, and now he is aiming for a 15 per cent cut. Prime Minister Churchill tried to effect a similar reduction in Great Britain. The Australian government is trying to cut defence expenditures by 8 per cent.
In recent months I believe the construction of airport buildings, military buildings and the like, has pretty well neared completion. Under these circumstances I believe that our defence effort could safely be cut at this time, without impairing efficiency, by perhaps $200 million.
In conclusion I repeat that the time has come when the Canadian people do want tax cuts. I also know that they cannot have tax cuts unless we have reduced expenditures. Taxes at the three levels of government today are taking one-third of our net national income. That fact is jeopardizing our trade position abroad and is contributing to unemployment at home. I call upon the federal government to set an example to Canadian industry, by improving its own efficiency, by cutting its own expenditures and reducing its own costs. If it will set such an example, then and only then is it fair for the minister to tell Canadian business to compete by becoming more efficient.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, subject to only one minor incidental exception that I remember, it has not been the practice for me to take any personal part in the debate on the budget. The government's proposals and its policies with respect to the budget are put forward by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), and in doing so he speaks for each and every one of his colleagues.
Now, this year, as in the past, the Minister of Finance has done that in a manner which in fact as well as because of our joint constitutional responsibility has the full and unqualified support of each and every one
The Budget-Mr. St. Laurent of us. There has arisen, however, an unfortunate clash over the use of direct taxing powers by the federal authorities and the authorities of the province of Quebec. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) on two occasions already has suggested that this clash is such as to make it my duty, as Prime Minister, to invite all the provincial governments to meet with the federal authorities to deal with it. I feel that I should make a short statement to the house-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege, I cannot let that statement go unchallenged. I have at no time said that it was necessary to call the premiers together to resolve the problem that has arisen with Quebec. What I said was that this problem affected all the provinces and that all the provinces should be brought together to discuss the broad question of taxation, which it is the duty of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) to resolve in some way in view of the promises made.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Speaker, I stand corrected if there is any correction in what the hon. gentleman has said.
I feel that I should make a short statement to the house on my position as Prime Minister with respect to the suggestion of the Leader of the Opposition, whether it be expressed in my terms or, if he prefers, in his terms.
This clash in federal-provincial relations is not something new. It should not be forgotten that its resurgence at this time is not the result of any recent action of the federal government. It arises as the result of a statute recently adopted by the legislature of Quebec imposing taxes on the personal incomes of a certain number of Quebec taxpayers who are also taxed under the federal Income Tax Act.
The provincial statute contains an assertion that under the constitution the provincial governments have priority over the federal government in this field of direct taxation. This recent action follows the serious attempt made in the dominion-provincial fiscal conference of December, 1950, to find and to implement a satisfactory solution of the problem arising out of the present needs of the federal and provincial authorities, and their concurrent taxing powers over the same taxpayers. It might be interesting to compare this assertion of priority of right in the field of direct taxation with what I think is a quite frank and realistic attitude taken at this 1950 conference by another provincial government, that of Ontario.

The Budget-Mr. St. Laurent
We find in the report of the proceedings of the conference at page 22 that Mr. Frost said the following in that connection:
In the past there has been a great deal of discussion over the respective rights of our federal government and our provinces in the various fields of taxation. The federal government has an unquestioned right in the field of indirect taxation. The field of direct taxation has been divided. The opinion of Sir Thomas White when he imposed the first federal income tax in 1917 has often been quoted. He stated that because the provinces and, in consequence, their municipalities were confined in the raising of revenues to the measures of direct taxation the federal government should not, except in a case of "manifest public necessity", invade the fields to which the provinces were solely confined for the purpose of raising their revenue. He indeed indicated that in entering the field of income tax the federal government was violating the spirit though not the law of the confederation arrangement.
Mr. Frost then went on:
We believe that we must be realistic about these matters. In 1950 we are living in a different world than that of 1917. We do not think it is possible for the federal government to withdraw from the fields of personal income or corporation tax. They derive a great portion of their revenue from these fields and they are indispensable to them. What is needed is the frank recognition that there must be a joint occupation of these fields and with this recognition an active spirit of cooperation between the provincial and federal governments. The federal system of government is a partnership and if it is to operate efficiently it must be a working partnership. We believe that ways and means of either assigning or sharing these fields of taxation can be devised which will be mutually satisfactory to the federal government as well as to the provinces. After all, such a recognition carries with it the realization that both federal and provincial taxes come from the same source, namely, the Canadian taxpayer.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not believe anyone can dispute that the federal government does derive a great portion of its revenues from these fields. In fact, the taxes from these fields yield almost 60 per cent of the total federal revenue, about $2-5 billion of total revenues of something less than $4-5 billion.
Now, are those revenues indispensable to the discharge of the federal government's national responsibilities? To get an answer to this question, we have only to remember that the debt charges amount to about half a billion dollars; that federal subsidies and tax rental payments to the provinces amount to about $340 million; that defence and defence production expenditures amount to almost $2 billion-$1,900 million; and that welfare expenditures disbursed by the Department of National Health and Welfare and by the Department of Veterans Affairs amount to almost a billion dollars. Well, that represents almost four-fifths, almost 80 per cent of the total federal expenditures. I feel everyone will admit that all these are national

responsibilities, have become national responsibilities, and that provision for them has to be made.
I am not disputing that the provinces and municipalities also have pressing fiscal needs.
I am merely saying that Mr. Frost's realistic statement of December 1950 is still true as a realistic appraisal of the situation now. It is true also that the federal system is necessarily and inevitably a partnership, and if it is to work efficiently it must be a working partnership. We tried our best at the expiry of the wartime tax agreements, and again in 1950, to devise a method whereby our system could operate as a working partnership, based on that frank recognition of the fact that our fiscal needs were such that there had to be joint occupation of the field of corporate and personal income tax or an appropriate sharing of the revenues derived from that field.
On the other hand it is not in agreement with the facts to say that the federal government failed to recognize its undertaking given when the wartime agreements were made, that they would be only temporary agreements. They were only temporary agreements and they came to an end. But the problem did not come to an end and because it did not come to an end we tried to devise some way of meeting it, and having found that our so-called green book proposals were not acceptable to some of the provincial governments we offered to renew the wartime tax rental agreements on a basis which provided a larger share of the revenue to the provinces than during the years of the war. No province had to make a new agreement, and as a matter of fact the two largest provinces did not make any new tax rental agreement, although seven of the then nine provinces chose to make them and they were authorized by acts of parliament and of the legislatures and became operative. But they were all temporary agreements and it had been one of the undertakings at the time they were being discussed and being prepared for signature that there would be another dominion-provincial fiscal conference at least a year before they expired to determine what would happen when they again came to an end.
That conference took place in December 1950 though the agreements were still to operate until March 31, 1952, 15 or 16 months before the expiry of the agreements. In December 1950 the situation was as described by Mr. Frost in his opening speech at that 1950 conference, and we could think of nothing better to suggest than a further renewal, because the problem was still there. We did make that suggestion, but we did

not pretend that these tax rental agreements were an ideal solution nor that they should or could be a permanent solution, but we had been unable to devise anything that was apt to work out as satisfactorily under the conditions which existed at that time. We and others felt that there was some merit in a system of sharing the proceeds of these taxes on a fair basis rather than having each one of two or more authorities imposing and collecting taxes from the same taxpayers in the same field.
No other scheme was discussed, though some of the provincial premiers expressed their dislike of having what they referred to as subsidies instead of exercising the responsibility of levying their own taxes. Most of the provinces, however, favoured the renewal agreements, and even the premier of Ontario, who had had no agreement since the expiry of the wartime agreement, expressed these views concerning the fiscal arrangements:
... I believe that these must be framed against the background of the emergent and, I hone, transient conditions to which I have referred.
We are experiencing inflation. The cost of government, as of other things, is rising. We cannot say where prices will be a year from now. let alone four or five years from now. Under these conditions we should try to avoid making decisions which will commit us irrevocably to a course from which we might find it impossible or impracticable to retrace our steps. I suggest in view of the emergent conditions through which we are passing that we endeavour to proceed to an agreement or agreements on the grounds of finding mutually satisfactory methods for the next few years which will meet the substantial requirements of the federal government and those of the provinces without making irrevocably basic alterations in our relationships.
We now have the experience of the last four years in which eight of the provinces have participated in tax rental agreements with the federal government.
Newfoundland had come in in the meantime and it had made a tax rental agreement but there was none with Ontario or Quebec.
These tax agreements have filled a need in Canada. They have been of considerable assistance to several of the provinces, and it is likely they will continue in some form to have a place in the arrangements which will be made here.
A little further on in his speech he said:
Perhaps the needs of all the provinces for the next few years would be met if we were to revise the present plan in some particulars to encourage certain improvements which experience now shows would be desirable. Probably it would be better to follow this course rather than to attempt at this time to create something which would be entirely new and untried.
After the opening speeches of the conference which are reported in the published report, the conference resolved itself into a committee of the whole to sit and discuss in camera. The only published record of what
The Budget-Mr. St. Laurent took place in the in-camera discussions is the offer which was submitted by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) and his explanatory statement about that offer followed by the release of the agreed statement to the press which was issued and published after the in-camera sessions had been adjourned. That is to be found at page 137 of the published report of the conference and it is in these terms:
The conference discussed:
1.	The offer of the federal government for new tax agreements;
2.	The offer of the federal government respecting old age security.
3.	A provincial proposal for an amendment to the constitution to permit the provincial legislature to levy an indirect sales tax at the retail level.
It will be remembered that at that time there was also being discussed at this fiscal conference the proposal for the universal old age pension scheme which would require an amendment to the constitution, and apparently there also had been discussed the suggestion of an amendment which would permit the provincial legislatures to levy indirect taxes at the retail level.
The statement goes on:
It was agreed:
That the proposed amendments to the constitution regarding this indirect tax and regarding old age pensions should be drafted by the Department of Justice and submitted to the provincial governments for early consideration;
That a continuing committee should be set up to consider the character of legislation which would be appropriate respecting persons between the ages of 65 and 69 and to what groups thereof and under what conditions it should be made applicable in each province;
That the continuing committee should be under the chairmanship of the Minister of National Health and Welfare and should be brought together as soon as provincial decisions had been reached on the constitutional amendment;
I believe the constitutional amendment referred to in that last paragraph was the one which would be required to provide for the old age pension.
The statement continues:
And that the provincial governments would consider the proposal for new tax agreements and indicate their respective positions at a later date.
It was also decided to suspend the further deliberations of the federal-provincial conference on constitutional amendment and of its continuing committee of attorneys-general pending consideration of the tax agreements and related matters. Once these have been disposed of, the committee of attorneys-general will resume its deliberations at the earliest convenience of the federal and provincial governments.
Here I digress for a moment to call attention to the fact that this is the explanation of the fact that the federal-provincial conference on constitutional amendment and the continuing committee of attorneys general have not met since that time. It was agreed
4338	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. St. Laurent that their deliberations would be suspended. It must be recalled that that conference had nothing to do with any other actual amendment to the constitution than the provision of a method whereby subsequent amendments could be made here in Canada without having to be referred to the parliament of the United Kingdom. It was realized that that was something that was desirable but not urgent and something about which it was not apt to be possible to reach any agreement if we could not reach an agreement on the immediately urgent fiscal problems that we had to deal with. Hon. members know that those fiscal problems and the matters relating to them have not yet been disposed of. Of that fact there can be no better evidence than the turn which part of this debate has taken on the present budget.
But with respect to the tax rental proposals I was of the opinion-as I still am-that these temporary agreements were, under the circumstances, good agreements; I was of the opinion that they were good for Canada and good for each one of the provinces. They recognized and gave effect to the concurrent rights of Canada and of the provinces in this field of direct taxes. I do not think that they impaired in any way the constitutional jurisdiction either of parliament or of the legislatures of the provinces. They also provided that, while they were in force, the people of each province would have for their provincial services a fair share of the kind of taxes which are made possible by the general economic activity of the Canadian nation, although for collection purposes they cannot be evenly productive throughout the whole country. I can assure the house that if I had felt that the agreements could have meant any permanent impairment of either federal or provincial jurisdiction, I would not have been prepared to recommend them.
The situation at the present time is such that I think it would be a grave responsibility to make any permanent change in what was provided by the original act of 1867. That does not mean that there cannot be agreed to from time to time a modus vivendi as to the way in which the respective powers of the federal authorities and the provincial authorities will be exercised. But I cannot bring myself to believe that I would be prepared to take the responsibility of any permanent alteration in the constitutional powers as they were allocated between the federal authorities and the provincial authorities at the time of confederation.
I happen to be-as I happened to be in 1950 -the Prime Minister of Canada, but I am a resident of Quebec; and I am just as firm a believer in the integrity of our federal system


with its division of powers and responsibility as is any other Canadian, whether he is a resident of Quebec or of any other province. Both as Prime Minister and as a resident of Quebec I would have been happy to see my native province participate in this modus vivendi because I did not see nor can I now see in it any danger or threat to either federal or provincial constitutional rights.
The statement agreed to after the incamera discussions, and published at that time, was that each province would consider these tax rental proposals and would indicate its position at a later date. There followed a great many more negotiations between the Department of Finance and the individual provinces, and within eighteen months or so nine of the ten provinces indicated their respective positions and entered into the proposed temporary rental agreements which are to extend to March 31, 1957. The government of Quebec did not do so, however. It just abstained from having any further dealings or discussion with us about the matter in any way or form whatsoever. I saw in the Montreal Star some time ago a report that Mr. Duplessis said that he had written to me and to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott). He may have written to me and to the Minister of Finance, but not about any solution of the fiscal problems between the federal authorities and Quebec, unless he is referring to some correspondence we had when we were discussing the grants to universities. In one of those letters he said this: Why do you not turn over to me 5 per cent of the personal income tax? That will be more than you are offering to Quebec universities under this $7 million grant. I replied that this grant would expire on March 31. I do not remember just the date of the correspondence but it was some little time before March 31. I said: You know that under the present act we cannot make any remission of this 5 per cent of income tax to the provincial government. We could merely give it as a deduction to a taxpayer who had paid a provincial income tax to your government. The other thing is the constitutional lapsing of this vote unless: Quebec's share is taken from it before March 31. Can we not find some scheme which will not prejudice your position or ours but which will not leave these Quebec institutions without their proportion of this grant which is about to lapse? For that year an arrangement was worked out whereby there was a joint commission of the federal government and the provincial government to makefile allocation and to recommend a way in which the grant would be paid to the institutions in Quebec. But that had nothing:

to do with the general possible collision between the exercise of federal rights and the exercise of provincial rights in the field of direct taxes.
Then, as the house knows, a few weeks ago, without any suggestion whatsoever from the Quebec government that some kind of agreed working arrangement with the federal government might be desirable, the Quebec legislature passed this taxing statute which is in force and which gives rise to this controversy. It is in force and those of us who reside in Quebec must comply with it. Like many others, no doubt, I myself have commenced to comply with it and have made my first quarterly payment in accordance with its terms. Under the legislation as it exists, and as it was known to exist at the time that the Quebec statute was passed, we who are taxed by it will be entitled, when we settle our 1954 federal income tax, to a credit not exceeding 5 per cent of the federal income tax, though the provincial tax amounts to 15 per cent or more. According to my calculation-I may be leaning backwards-it is something over 16 per cent in my case. Of course no one likes the idea of having to pay about 10 per cent more income tax because he resides in the province of Quebec than if he resided elsewhere. The question arises: What can be done about it? Well, it is my opinion, Mr. Speaker, that anything which can be done about it will have to be the result of some kind of temporary agreement between the federal authorities and the Quebec authorities. I hope it is not the view of the Quebec authorities that there cannot be any kind of agreement with the federal authorities because of the danger of impairing what they claim to be involved in the autonomy of Quebec. I hope they do not feel that there could not even be any exploratory negotiations with us, but if that were the situation I do not see how there is any way of avoiding the consequences of this clash.
Surely no one will suggest that this parliament should agree or could agree to recognize the asserted claim of Quebec's priority of rights over the rights of the nation as a whole in the field of corporation and personal income taxes. If the fathers of confederation had been so unwise as to make that the law of the constitution, of course we would have to get along with it as best we could in spite of its paralysing effect upon the nation as a whole. But fortunately it is not the law of the constitution and this government and this parliament, I am sure, are too conscious of our respective responsibilities to the nation as a whole, the nation
The Budget-Mr. St. Laurent of today and the nation of future generations, to do anything that would tend to make that the law of the constitution.
What then is the alternative? The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) has suggested, perhaps not as a complete alternative but as something that should be done, that there should be a federal-provincial conference. Well, what reason is there for bringing together the representatives of the other provinces? The other provinces have all made tax rental agreements which still have about three years to run. These agreements were entered into in good faith. They were entered into under the authority of acts of parliament and of the legislatures of the respective provinces, and I think Canada has got to live up to them unless they are modified by mutual consent.
This government is not going to suggest to the provinces that have made these agreements that they should consider modifying them unless we have got some better reason for doing so than the mere fact that one of its provinces has not made a similar agreement and has proceeded to levy its own taxes without any agreement at all. No one will suggest, I am sure, that the federal government should or could give preferential treatment to any one province. I think we would all feel that just could not be done. No one, I hope, would suggest, in order to give Quebec taxpayers more generous deductions than those now provided for in our income tax law, that we should either increase the tax rental payments to the other provinces or agree that they too may impose their own taxes and get for their taxpayers, at the very substantially increased expense of the federal treasury, somewhat more generous deductions. The federal treasury just could not stand either of those courses.
On the other hand, I think that everybody hopes some temporary arrangement can be worked out which will enable the people of Quebec to get for their province's services a fair share of the taxes on corporate and personal incomes without having to bear income tax burdens greater than those which prevail elsewhere in Canada. How that eminently desirable result can be achieved in some other way than through the way agreed to by the other provinces I do not know, but there may be alternatives. I hope there are alternatives. Since the taxing statute was passed many individuals and groups of individuals have had thoughts and made suggestions about possible alternatives. One proposal has been put before the provincial commission on constitutional problems by the institute of chartered accountants of Quebec.

The Budget-Mr. H. O. White I have not seen their brief, but the Montreal Star in its issue of April 27, 1954, had this to say about it:
It proposed a sweeping revision and a sharing of tax fields along lines which may, or may not,
be adapted to the national need but which deserves study just the same.
The Gazette of Saturday, May 1, reported that the Montreal board of trade had also submitted a brief to the same commission. The report reads:
The Montreal board of trade proposed yesterday that the Quebec royal commission on constitutional problems prepare immediately an interim report on income and corporation taxes and urge the provincial government to confer promptly with federal government representatives to find a satisfactory compromise to end an "intolerable situation". In a brief presented at a commission sitting here, the board said it believes the matters in dispute must and can be settled by negotiation without impairment of the constitutional rights of the province, "provided the negotiations are approached in a spirit of good will and having in mind the interests of the taxpayer".
I am sure any negotiations would be approached in a spirit of good will and having in mind the interests of both the federal and provincial governments and the very pertinent fact that those interests affect the same taxpayers of both levels of government. Briefs have also been submitted by the chamber of commerce and many other public bodies and, as I have said, we ourselves have had representations from many individuals and groups who are concerned, as we all are, about this problem.
But the only authority we can recognize as entitled to make suggestions for the province of Quebec is the Quebec government. I think that is self-evident, and that is why the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) stated in his budget speech that if there was a desire for co-operation and collaboration the premier of Quebec would always find the door open for full and frank discussion in the hope of finding a mutually satisfactory solution. Some persons, both in this house and outside of it, have tried to describe that as an invitation to the premier of Quebec to come cap in hand knocking at the federal door. Of course it is nothing of the kind, and I do not think it is helpful to try to so distort it. It was and it remains a sincere and genuine expression of readiness at all times to sit down with the authorities of Quebec for a full and frank discussion of any alternative to a tax rental agreement and the hope that they will indicate their readiness to do so too. It implied our further hope that through these discussions we might be able to find a mutually satisfactory solution. That is, of course, still our position, and those are still our hopes.


If, after negotiations between us and the Quebec authorities, it appears that there is some kind of modus vivendi which could be agreed to between us and which would respect the rights of both the federal and provincial authorities, and which could be offered to other provinces or any of them, in lieu of their present tax rental agreements, and still leave the federal government in a position to discharge its national obligations, I would not hesitate a moment to invite representatives of all the provinces to meet with us in another conference. But, quite frankly, I do not think that under any other conditions the holding of a federal-provincial conference now would be desirable, or apt to be at all helpful.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at this moment I do not propose to discuss any of the problems with which the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has just dealt. I am going to leave that to those who have made a study of federal-provincial affairs.
I do wish to say that I appreciate what was said by the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre (Mr. Thatcher) regarding the budget and the savings that could and should be made in the administration of our affairs so that the Canadian taxpayer, whether he be a manufacturer, a farmer, or engaged in any other occupation, could lower his costs of production.
I rise today to protest against budget resolution No. 6 in the amendments suggested to the Income Tax Act. It reads as follows:
For the taxation of a resident mutual insurance corporation, other than a life insurance corporation, as though the surplus arising from its insurance activities on and after January 1, 1954, were a profit from a business, and declaring that a non-resident mutual insurance corporation, other than a life insurance corporation, shall be deemed to be and always to have been subject to taxation on that basis.
I was one who thought that when the Supreme Court of Canada ruled on the case of the Stanley Mutual of New Brunswick this question of taxation of farm mutuals was a closed book. However the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) has seen fit to introduce it in his budget, for reasons which I cannot quite understand.
First of all, what I do understand is that from that proposed taxation only about $130,000 could be expected. When one thinks of that amount and compares it with the hundreds of millions of dollars the government is taking from the people, and spending, he realizes at once that it is only a small pittance. And it is for this reason I rise in my place today to voice my protest against resolution No. 6.

I do so, first, because in their long history the farm mutual fire insurance companies have provided fire insurance at cost to their policyholders-and I say "at cost" and not at a profit. Never in their long history have they indicated a profit.
I protest in the second place because this move would aid in the final and eventual elimination of many of the farm mutual insurance companies.
Thirdly, I protest because the minister has not seen fit to accept the ruling of the Supreme Court of Canada in the case of the Stanley Mutual in the province of New Brunswick.
Fourth, I rise to protest because the minister failed to take into consideration the fact that in addition to the premium they pay, the farmers and others insured must also sign a premium note to the extent of a percentage of the face value of the policy. And the premium note is for no other purpose than to share in the losses-not in the profits-that might come to policyholders of mutual insurance companies, and to assist in their financing.
I understand there are about sixty-eight local mutual companies operating in Ontario. They operate in areas where in most cases fire-fighting equipment is either inadequate or non-existent. Therefore they are taking risks that many straight line companies do not take, and do not care to take.
Then this question arises in my mind: Who are the real culprits behind the minister who are so insistent that budget resolution No. 6 shall be proceeded with? Through the years the premiums paid by farmers on their policies have varied according to the costs of providing the insurance. But, as I say, there has always been the premium note which has stood as a guarantee against loss. Surely, of all people, the minister is or should be aware of the fact that mutual fire insurance companies, as in respect of other companies, must have reserves with which to operate.
I think this is an ill-conceived move and one that should be dropped. And I am not alone in this, because members on all sides of the house know of the plight of these insurance companies and of the resolution, and are just as perturbed as 1 am about the final and net result which, in many cases, would mean the elimination of small farm mutuals, some of which have been in operation since prior to confederation.
