speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the refusal of the government to grant the income tax deduction requested by the taxpayers of the province of Quebec
The Budget-Mr. Gagnon brings once again to light the matter of the rights of the central government and of the provincial legislatures.
It therefore seems appropriate to recall the debates that preceded and followed the pact of 1867, to stress certain statements made at that time and in the years that followed and to analyse the decisions brought down by the courts in that matter.
The arguments I wish to submit today to the kind attention of this house lead me to believe and to assert that the provinces have a prior right in the field of direct taxation. In support of that theory, which is not new, I would like to quote the opinion of a few legal lights and political leaders. I have taken those statements from works pertaining to constitutional problems.
During the debate on second reading of the act of 1867 in the House of Lords, Lord Carnarvon, who had helped the Canadian delegates put the finishing touches to the document, stated:
(Text):
The several provinces which are now free to raise a revenue as they may think fit, surrender to the central parliament all powers under this head except that of direct taxation . . . But there is, as I have said, a concurrent power of legislation to be exercised by the central and the local parliament. It extends over three separate subjects-immigration, agriculture, public works.
(Translation):
In the case of the Liquidators of the Maritime Bank of Canada v. the Receiver General of New Brunswick, Lord Watson clearly defined the character of our constitution and the status of the federal and provincial governments:
(Text):
The object of the British North America Act was neither to weld the provinces into one, nor to subordinate provincial governments to a central authority, but to create a federal government in which they should all be represented, entrusted with the exclusive administration of affairs in which they had a common interest, each province retaining its independence and autonomy ... In so far as regards those matters which by section 92 are specially reserved for provincial legislation, the legislation of each province continues to be free from the control of the dominion, and as supreme as it was before the passing of the act . . .
The provincial legislature possesses powers not of administration merely but of legislation in the strictest sense of that word; and within the limits assigned by section 92, of the act of 1867, these powers are exclusive and supreme.
(Translation):
To those who contended that the British North America Act broke all ties between the crown and the provinces, the privy council answered that the latter were not subordinated to a federal government, and reasserted the supremacy of the province in matters reserved for provincial authority.

The Budget-Mr. Gagnon
(Text):
And, in Hodge v. the Queen, Spragge, C.J.,
says:
The provinces had possessed plenary powers upon subjects of a local and domestic nature before confederation; and the general scheme of confederation appears to have been to leave to them the plenary control of these subjects. They were, under the act, legislatures in regard to these subjects in the true and full sense of the term. This is the more apparent from the use of the words "exclusive" and "exclusively" (and they are used repeatedly), in the imperial act.
The following passage from the argument of Mr. Edward Blake before the privy council in St. Catharines Milling and Lumber Co. v. the Queen, may be quoted in this connection:
What then was the general scheme of the act? First of all, as I have suggested, it was to create a federal, as distinguished from a legislative union: but a union composed of several existing and continued entities. It was not the intention of parliament to mutilate, confound and destroy the provinces mentioned in the preamble, and, having done so, from their mangled remains, stewed in some legislative cauldron, to evoke by some legislative incantation absolutely new provinces into an absolutely new existence. It was rather, I submit, the design and object of the act, so far as was consistent with the redivision of the then province of united Canada into its old political parts. Upper and Lower Canada, and with the federal union of the four entities. Nova Scotia. New Brunswick and the resettled parts of old Canada, Ontario and Quebec-it was the design I say, so far as was consistent with these objects, by gentle and considerate treatment to preserve the vital breath and continue the political existence of the old provinces. However this may be, they were being made, as has been well said, not fractions of a unit, but units of a multiple . . .
(Translation):
Sir Alexander Galt, who had advocated legislative union in a speech delivered in Toronto, nevertheless made the following statement during the parliamentary debates of 1865:
(Text):
In transferring to the general government all the large sources of revenue, and in placing in their hand with a single exception, that of direct taxation, all the means whereby the industry of the people may be made to contribute to the wants of the state . . .
(Translation):
Remembering that Galt was then minister of finance in the Canadian legislature, and, as such, entrusted with the estimates of the new provinces, that he was one of the men most responsible for the pact of 1867, moreover, that he was a known centralizer, we realize that even the advocates of a strong central authority were giving up direct taxation exclusively to the provinces. It was then a source of revenue of little importance, quite unpopular-just as it is today-which they thought it was almost impossible, or at least very difficult, to put into force.


During the 1867-1917 period, as I said here recently, the central power, recognizing the exclusive rights of the provinces, abstained from encroaching upon that field.
(Text):
As Mr. Benjamin observed upon the argument in Russell v. the Queen before the privy council on May 2, 1882, referring to sections 91 and 92:
The general rule of construction is one of course which your Lordships will keep in view, that general words are controlled by special and specific provisions; that you do not take general words to override special provisions, but you take special provisions as constituting in their nature exceptions to the general words.
(Translation):
The reference at the time was to the right of Ottawa to regulate the liquor trade.
In the case of Bank of Toronto v. Lambe, this point of view would seem to have been approved.
(Text):
Their Lordships adhere to that view, and hold that, as regards direct taxation within the province to raise revenue for provincial purposes, that subject falls wholly within the jurisdiction of the provincial legislatures.
(Translation):
Before the Supreme Court, Mr. Justice Sedgwick, in the Local Prohibition case, expressed the view that the act is an agreement, a treaty, a pact concluded by independent communities upon federating. He says:
(Text):
When a general subject is assigned to one legislature, whether federal or provincial, and a particular subject forming part or carved out of that general subject is assigned to the other legislature, the exclusive right of legislation, in respect to the particular subject, is with the latter legislature. For example, parliament has marriage, but the legislatures have the solemnization of marriage. On that subject they are paramount and supreme.
(Translation):
And so, any particular matter handed over to a province may not be absorbed by a general matter handed over to the federal government, even though one would be included in the other.
Lord Watson, to explain his interpretation of sections 91 and 92, in that case, states:
Any other interpretation of the general authority devolved upon the Canadian parliament by section 91, in addition to the powers therein enumerated, would not only be contrary to the intention of the act, in Their Lordships' opinion, but would also be tantamount to divesting the provinces of any autonomy.
Clement, in "The Law of Canadian Constitution", at pages 480 and 481 clearly stated that the particular excludes the general:

(Text):
From any large general class in either section must be excepted any particular class in the other which forms a branch or subdivision of the larger general class.
For example:	from the general class
"criminal law (sec. 91, no. 27)" must be excepted the particular class, provincial penal law, sec. 92-15.
From the "regulation of trade and commerce, section 91, subsection 2, must be excepted trade "licences", section 92-9. From "property and civil rights," section 92, subsection 13, must be excepted many items contained in section 91. From "the administration of justice in the province" must be excepted certain branches of jurisprudence which are to be found wrapped up in some of the items in section 91.
It has, indeed, been suggested that all the items of section 92 are in the nature of exception to section 91; but, while there is a sense in which the proposition is certainly true, it is equally certain that in the sense of the rules under discussion some of the items in section 91 are particular classes to be excepted out of larger general classes enumerated in section 92.
(Translation):
In the case of Citizens Insurance Co. v. Parsons, in 1880, Judge Montague Smith analysed the potential conflicts between the subject matters of section 91 and those of section 92.
(Text):
He believes that the legislature could not have intended that the powers exclusively assigned to the provincial legislatures should be absorbed in those given to the dominion parliament. He gives as an example the celebration of marriage in a province and direct taxation. He adds:
... so the raising of money by any mode or system of taxation is enumerated among the classes of subject in section 91; . . .
But direct taxation within the province in order to raise revenue for provincial purposes has been assigned to the provincial legislatures by section 92, so it obviously could not have been intended that in this instance also the general power should override the particular one.
(Translation):
A general power cannot include a particular power which flows from it.
In the case of Hodge v. the Queen, in 1883, the privy council refused to recognize that provincial parliaments were inferior institutions. Their Lordships stated that, within the limits of the subject matters and 83276-274J
The Budget-Mr. Gagnon fields mentioned in section 92, "the local legislature wields a supreme power and enjoys the same authority as the dominion parliament". This may be found at page 59 of the report of the royal commission:
Sovereignty resides in the state. Central and local governments are the agents of that sovereignty and they cannot destroy or control each other.
(Text):
Joseph Doutre in "Constitution of Canada", page 222, says:
According to the well-known rule where a general intention is expressed in a statute and the act also expresses a particular intention incompatible with the general intention, the particular intention shall be considered as an exception," direct taxation must be considered by section 92 as being excepted from the monopoly given in general terms by 91st section to the federal parliament.
Bora Laskin, professor of law at the University of Toronto, in Canadian Constitutional Law, Toronto, 1951, notes that the respective taxing authority of dominion and provinces may not be used by either of them to sterilize powers of the other government. (Translation):
If the federal government had a prior right in the field of direct taxation, the provinces would, in fact, be deprived of this source of revenue and, in spite of the explicit terms of section 92 (2), would be unable to make use of it.
We cannot maintain Canadian federalism without autonomous provinces, and our provinces would not be autonomous if they could not keep their financial independence.
Obviously, powers assigned solely to the provincial legislatures must not be absorbed by the powers granted to the dominion parliament.
(Text):
In re Regulation and Control of Aeronautics in Canada (1932) A.C. 54, Lord Sankey, L.C., stated that:
Inasmuch as the act embodies a compromise under which the original provinces agreed to federate, it is important to keep in mind that the preservation of the rights of minorities was a condition on which such minorities entered into the federation, and the foundation upon which the whole structure was subsequently erected. The process of interpretation as the years go on ought not to be allowed to dim or to whittle down the provisions of the original contract upon which the federation was founded, nor is it legitimate that any judicial construction of the provisions of sections 91 and 92 should impose a new and different contract upon the federating bodies. (Translation):
If this is a compromise, Mr. Speaker, each power is a sovereign power within the limits of its attributions.
Sections 91 and 92 are mutually exclusive.
Section 95 confers on the dominion and on the provinces a joint responsibility with

The Budget-Mr. Gagnon regard to agriculture and immigration, with a predominance of federal authority in case of disputes.
The constitution has therefore given to the central government, in matters pertaining to taxation, powers which are limited by those granted to the provincial states. The latter have thus the exclusive power to levy direct taxes within the limits of their respective territory for provincial purposes. "The theory of the federal government's unlimited rights crushes, in its very principle, the fiscal autonomy of the provinces."
Such a conception is definitely anti-federative. A federation is not based upon the principle that one of the partners can alter the conditions of the federation or destroy it but upon a pre-established equilibrium that can be modified through evolution without any of the parties having the power to break it of its own initiative.
Through centralization of revenue sources and an almost absolute control of financial, social, and economic legislation, the Ottawa government is endeavouring to establish a national spirit which can result in a consolidation of its position but also, on the other hand, in the destruction of the loyalty of the taxpayers towards the local governments.
Some of the provinces may like to be nothing more than pensioners but the province of Quebec is not one of them. Following the example set by our ancestors, we are proud enough to refuse to be valets.
He who holds the purse strings holds every initiative, every liberality and the most powerful means to reduce refractory elements to acceptance of his ideas.
Professor Adarkar, Ph.B., in "The Principles and Problems of Federal Finance" (London, 1933), establishes a distinction between political sovereignty and legal-in principle-sovereignty. He holds that financial sovereignty determines political sovereignty, whatever the situation in respect to legal sovereignty may be.
(Text):
Mr. W. A. Carrothers, from Victoria, in "Problems of the Canadian Federation" published in Canadian Journal of Economics and Political Science, February 1935, states at page 28:
Political sovereignty would be of little value without commensurate financial authority: otherwise a government would be unable to implement its own legislation.
Mr. J. A. Corry, of Queen's University, editor of the same publication, in an article entitled "The Federal Dilemma", volume 7, page 26, 1941, says:
The wide taxing powers of the federal government, if resolutely used will help to whip the states into line.

(Translation):
Since the federal authorities cannot legislate in one way for French-speaking Canadians and in another for the other citizens of the country, it becomes important that "the province of Quebec which is, de jure and de facto, the legal and political habitat of French-speaking Canadians" have and maintain the necessary executive, judicial and legislative powers as well as the revenues for the good administration of the rights and privileges which belong to her exclusively.
Those privileges, essential to the survival of our racial group, have been guaranteed to us by the pact of 1867 and any encroachment upon Quebec's autonomy amounts to a breach of the contract between the two great races of this country.
Authorities agree that section 92, subsection 13-pertaining to property and civil rights in the province-was included in the act of federation for the sole purpose of-
-safeguarding the fundamental institutions and ways of life of Quebec.
That quotation is taken from page 34, volume 1, of the report of the royal commission on dominion-provincial relations.
The case of Quebec is truly unique in our federation. All provinces except Quebec have the British civil law. All except Quebec and Newfoundland have divorce courts. All except Quebec and Newfoundland have a system of neutral public schools. All provinces except Quebec have but one official language, English. Quebec is the only province with a legislative council. Finally, this province is the only one having a majority of its citizens who do not speak English, that is the French-speaking group.
One should not lose sight of that historical fact.
Any amendment to the constitution requires the consent of all contracting parties.
(Text):
On February 18, 1925 the then minister of justice, Mr. Lapointe, said as reported at page 298 of Hansard:
. . . the British North America Act itself is not only the charter of the Dominion of Canada: it is just as much the charter of the provinces of Canada. We derive our powers from the British North America Act; so do the provinces. They have no constitution other than the British North America Act; all their powers they derive from that act. Would it then be fair for us to arrogate to ourselves the right to change the act which is just as much the constitution of the provinces as it is our own?
. . . the conclusion is that we cannot ask for power to alter, without the consent of the provinces, the constitution which is their own constitution as well as it is ours. I ask my hon. friend this question. Confederation was achieved and the new parliament was opened in 1867. Does he believe that two years afterwards, in 1869. for

instance, this parliament could have fairly and reasonably amended the B.N.A. Act or have asked the imperial parliament to amend it, without the consent of the four original provinces? Could he fairly say that that could have been done two years after the opening of this parliament? If it could not be done at that time, could it be done 25 years afterwards, or even 50 years afterwards, without the consent of the contracting parties in the pact of confederation?
I heard it suggested some time ago that this idea at confederation of a treaty is an antiquated idea. Maybe it is. But truth does not cease to be truth when it gets old; and old truth is always true. You cannot prevent the facts from being facts whether you like them or not.
(Translation):
A dishonest practice aimed at drawing the sympathy or hatred of the ignorant and the anti-French elements, which has become popular in certain quarters through the insidious propaganda of centralizers, consists in painting the supporters of autonomy in the darkest colours and calling them separatists or isolationists.
However, nothing could be more false. What we are defending in rejecting legislative and fiscal absorption is the sacred right of remaining ourselves, of preserving our language, our religion, our ideals and our culture within the Canadian community.
(Text):
Referring to tax rental agreements in his budget speech last year the Minister of Finance said:
The virtue of this approach was that it was not dependent for success on the unanimous acceptance by all provinces. A cardinal principle in the offer was that no pressure, direct or indirect, should be placed on any province to accept an agreement. This has been a fundamental position in the federal government's attitude ever since.
(Translation):
Quebec, therefore, could, without running the risk of being blackmailed or criticized, refuse to sign the proposed agreement.
As for personal income tax, the federal legislation, recognizing that a provincial tax of that kind is possible and legitimate, allows specifically a 5 per cent deduction from the federal tax.
The central government thus recognizes, to a certain extent, the principle of deductibility.
To object, now, to this right being exercised, is to show open intention of forcing the province of Quebec to meet the requirements of the central power, which are opposed to the principles of sound democracy.
It is unjustifiable, we read in the brief submitted to the right hon. the Prime Minister of Canada by the chamber of commerce of the district of Montreal, to draw a distinction between a taxpayer entrusting the
The Budget-Mr. Gagnon federal government with remitting to the provinces a share of the taxes he has to pay, and the taxpayer who divides it himself.
The stand taken by the Prime Minister is no surprise to me, for he stated, at Winnipeg, in July 1953, that he didn't want to go down in history as the one responsible for depriving the federal government of powers that may be vitally needed to ensure our common salvation.
He prefers to take the responsibility of "undermining the federal pact, and surrendering the French Canadians to the majority", wrote Mr. Andre Laurendeau, after that statement was made. It is he who, as the legal adviser to the Rowell-Sirois commission, advocated a return to the first days of confederation, in other words, one fiscal authority in possession of all important revenues, and provinces supported by grants. It was also he who stated, in this very house, that the federal parliament could abolish section 133 of the constitution providing for the use of French in official documents, without the necessity of obtaining the prior consent of the provinces.
It would be impossible to imagine that those who drafted the agreement of 1867 would have wanted to bring about the disappearance of the provinces or to place them in such a position that they would be unable to benefit fully from the advantages of that sovereignty which they already possessed and to exercise those prerogatives devolved upon them by the act itself.
Those who represented at the time Lower Canada, that is, the province of Quebec, would never have signed a treaty divesting my fellow citizens of rights and revenues indispensable to their existence.
They knew in 1867 that in order to build schools, colleges and universities, government help was imperative; they knew that subsidies were necessary to preserve them, and still it was decided to leave to the provinces absolute authority on matters pertaining to education.
When offering subsidies to universities, the federal government recognized that they needed financial assistance. The step they then took in an unconstitutional way, why would they not take it indirectly, in the way advocated by the Quebec legislature, namely through allowing the deduction of the provincial tax from the federal tax. They would thus co-operate in the application of legislation designed to help those institutions.
For the central power, this is a nominal sum, $15 million at the most, taking into account the 5 per cent deduction already allowed and provided for by the act.
4346	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Gagnon
The Department of External Affairs will grant this year $31,450,000 to help other countries and international organizations and the Quebec taxpayers would be refused the few millions they claim?
Twenty-five million dollars are given under the Colombo plan in order to further the economical development of coutries in south and southeast Asia, but the legitimate claim of the people of Quebec is rejected.
Leopold Richer wrote on March 27, 1954, in Notre Temps:
Ottawa is acting as if it wanted open warfare or desired to crush the national unity which it pretends to build up and defend.
No concessions for Quebec, say the Liberals. No concessions for Quebec or the Vatican! But, on the other hand, let us make every possible concession to the communist governments and to Mao, the communist dictator of China!
That is how we are ruled. The Quebec Liberals betray the highest and most permanent interests of their province. They scarcely can be proud of such an attitude!
Like everybody else, judges have very different views, on political issues, says the royal commission report, at page 60. Should by any chance the present finance minister (Mr. Abbott) be appointed to the supreme court, it would be easy to foresee what rulings would be rendered in judicial disputes between the provinces and the central power.
The rights of the provinces in the field of direct taxation cannot be denied and autonomy becomes an empty word if the revenue essential to its preservation is not guaranteed through the granting of exclusive sources of revenue.
Notwithstanding the opinions of our fashionable "internationalists" and of our ambassadors of "good will", who are much more preoccupied with the fate of South Koreans or Indians than with the future of French Canadians in our confederation, the present struggle is not partisan in scope.
The main cause is the unjust and repeated encroachments of the Ottawa government on the fields allotted to the provinces. The struggle is that of those who ask for the integral respect of the 1867 contract between the two great races established in Canada, that of free men who cherish their financial and economic independence, without which it is impossible to exercise the other freedoms inherent to a sovereign state, that of people opposed to the dictatorship of socialist centralizers.
In that struggle, conducted not only for the benefit of the citizens of Quebec but for the welfare of all Canadians, we, of Quebec, are ready to fight until final victory is ours.
The people are on our side. We shall remain in the van as champions of provincial auton-


omy; we wish to prosper, but not by begging subsidies and alms from the government in Ottawa, not by being the servants of a wealthy but stingy master. We wish to work in peace and harmony with the central power, "to be united," as Talleyrand said "like a horse and its rider," provided the horse is not always the province of Quebec.
Let there be no barriers to our cultural development; let us have the necessary taxes to make our educational system prosper and, as always, Quebec will remain one of the glories of Canadian confederation.
Mr. Speaker, it is essential that the sacred interests of national unity and of our country should not be confused with the political interests of the Liberal party.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the occasion of my first speech, I would like to congratulate you upon your elevation to the high office of Speaker of the house.
The day a new member delivers his first speech is surely a day to be remembered. It is an opportunity for him to express the feelings which are a source of joy and satisfaction in the fulfilment of the duties he has assumed; it is also for him an opportunity of appraising some fearful aspects of the perspectives that open before him.
My first joy is, no doubt, to say how deeply honoured I am to represent in this house the good people of my constituency. The county of Kent, faithful to its tradition, once more indicated its confidence in the great Liberal party by sending me here to support this government, headed by a great leader, the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). Political history tells us that, since 1900, the county of Kent has been represented by a member of the Liberal party for forty years.
I therefore feel happy to uphold that tradition which, I hope, will be maintained for many more years.
The thought of those who preceded me in this house makes me fear the task I am beginning to fulfil, knowing that they have fulfilled theirs with brilliance and experience. But their example will be a source of inspiration to me, as I proceed forward along the path that lies ahead.
May I be allowed to mention at this point those predecessors of mine who are still alive. Many hon. members know with what zeal and devotion my immediate predecessor, the Hon. A. D. Leger, discharged his mandate during the thirteen years he spent in this house. It was to no one's surprise, such being the case, that his many years of

selfless service, his merit and his experience should have brought upon him the very great honour of being called upon to sit in the other place. Many hon. members here too will have known and appreciated the member who sat for Kent from 1935 to 1940, Mr. Louis P. Robichaud, of Richibucto. He has always devotedly served his county where he has been for a record breaking number of years a most diligent and devoted secretary-treasurer of the municipality of Kent. Some too will remember Mr. Telesphore Arsenault, who sat for Kent from 1930 to 1935. Mr. Arsenault, who is now over eighty years of age, also resides in Richibucto, loved and respected by all who know him. I also want to say a word about the member for Kent from 1911-17, Mr. Ferdinand Robidoux, a lawyer, who now resides at Shediac. Not only is he active in national causes, but he also is a devoted servant of his own municipal corporation. And without leaving the federal scene, I should also like to mention the name of Mr. Pius Michaud, who practises law in Edmundston, N.B.
Mr. Michaud sat in this chamber for seventeen years, and although he is 84 years old, he is still very active, and may I add that he has always been for me a most genial uncle. Here again, I want to recall the memory of the late Dr. E. N. Leger, federal member for Kent riding from 1890 to 1892, until his untimely death; the latter was my uncle, as well as the uncle of hon. Senator A. D. Leger. I now want to talk about the provincial political field, to recall the name of the Hon. A. A. Dysart, now judge of the New Brunswick court, former provincial member for Kent riding during 27 years, and premier of the province of New Brunswick from 1935 to 1940, and the memory of the late David Landry, former member for Kent from 1908 to 1917, who was successively minister of agriculture and provincial secretary-treasurer; he also was a most distinguished uncle of mine.
Mr. Speaker, Kent riding is part of the area called Acadia. Its people are also Acadians, to a large extent. So, as member for that riding and as an Acadian myself, I must talk now about the celebrations which will mark, in 1955, the bicentennial of the dispersion of the Acadians.
It is useless to retrace here the different stages of this historical event, the anniversary of which we want to stress. That, however, is not the aim of the celebrations that are being prepared. They will rather point out our rehabilitation as an ethnical group. What we shall try to demonstrate during these
The Budget-Mr. Michaud anniversary celebrations will not be so much the negative side of this historical fact, which would insist upon what the Acadian people was not to be, but rather the positive aspect, by showing what this people is now and what it is meant to become. The lessons we shall try to learn therefrom are related to our faith in our future. We shall spread, before today's generation, all the courage and strength our fathers needed in order to obtain for us the place we now occupy in this country of freedom, Canada. And in view of our past, we shall show the present generation tomorrow's duties and obligations. The Acadian people have only one ambition, that is to contribute, by the full development of qualities and gifts bestowed by Providence, to the cultural, economic and moral expansion of this country. Mr. Speaker, there is something more to this drama of dispersion. The fact that two countries, two races, which two centuries ago were full of animosity and hostility towards each other, have come closer together, in Europe as well as in America, and live in friendship and peace, is for the world, in these days of uncertainty and trouble, an invitation to universal peace addressed to men and countries of good will.
There are in America today from 1,200,000 to 1,400,000 Acadians: 600,000 in Louisiana;
300.000	in the maritimes; 150,000 in Quebec;
150.000	in New England; 50,000 in Ontario and the western provinces. Everywhere they profess the same faith, everywhere they sing the same hymn, "Ave Maria Stella", everywhere they fly the same flag, blue, white and red, with a gold star. Except in Louisiana and in the western provinces, the main Acadian communities are united under the banner of a fraternal society, the Assumption Society. That organization aims first of all at maintaining, through its branches, a sound solidarity, and, secondly, through its insurance fund, at ensuring a concentration of the savings of its members for their own protection and for the financing of their own Acadian enterprises.
The head office of that company is located in Moncton, New Brunswick. It is in the maritime provinces, in the very heart of Acadia of olden days, that Acadian life in its most ardent and authentic form is to be found. There we have prosperous, religious, educational and economic institutions which do honour to the whole country. Religious life is organized in one archdiocese and three Acadian dioceses: the archdiocese of Moncton, the dioceses of Edmundston, Bathurst and Yarmouth, the latter newly-formed. Numerous

The Budget-Mr. Michaud institutions look after our people's education. Among the most important, may I mention St. Joseph's university, Sacred Heart university at Bathurst, St. Louis university at Edmund-ston, Ste. Ann's college at Church Point, Notre-Dame d'Acadie college, at Moncton, and Maillet college at St. Basile, Madawaska. The two latter are classical colleges for girls.
Acadians also have their daily newspaper, L'Evangeline, founded through the generosity and with the help of everyone.
The French-language radio station recently set up at Moncton by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation gives much pride and satisfaction to the Acadian groups of the district. In the economic field, prosperous co-operative societies help their members to achieve economic independence.
Mr. Speaker, as an eminent man said just a few days ago: Acadia has risen; it is on the march. True, the Acadian population is still made up primarily of farmers and fishermen, who have always been in the forefront; but that group has its own institutions, its clergy, its professional classes and its leaders. Those are additional factors that ensure its survival.
Mr. Speaker, I have just given the house a brief outline of the Acadian people who will soon commemorate the bicentennial of the dispersion. The Acadian people invite all Canadians to join them during those celebrations. They urge the Canadian government and the governments of the provinces where Acadians are to be found to commemorate the event by appropriate deeds and acts.

As a maritimer, Mr. Speaker, I should now like to refer to different statements made in the house with regard to the economy of the maritime provinces. True it is that in the light of the general economy of our country there are reasons for a certain concern about our present conditions. As a stimulating measure some are advocating the Chignecto canal project for the purpose of increasing trade through our seaports. Others, viewing the need for more industrialization, are advocating the Passamaquoddy project as a means of providing more and cheaper power. Still others, in their own way, offer their own unbiased personal suggestions. But when all these proposals are made I am sure they are made with one common purpose in mind, to be of some assistance in devising ways and means to stimulate our maritime economy.

As a member from the maritimes I too have a keen desire to see that our provinces share more fully in, and contribute more effectively to, the fast expanding economy of our country. Perhaps I could illustrate to some extent the situation as it exists, if not in the whole of the maritimes at least in some parts, by relating to the house an incident which I personally witnessed a short time ago on the train to Ottawa. While I was sitting in my seat I could overhear the conversation of two young ladies sitting back of me. At a certain time I heard them speaking of a town that I knew very well, in the vicinity of my own home town. I then introduced myself and engaged in a conversation with them. I learned that the two ladies were the last members of a family of fourteen who had left their home town to take up domicile in a city west of our capital city. When I further questioned them as to the motives that had prompted the family to choose that particular city in preference to many others they gave me a still more significant answer. They said that they had chosen that city because half the people of their home town were already there. Our chief problem in many parts of the maritimes, Mr. Speaker, is a vital one. Unless we can hold at least the greater part of our natural increase of population we are faced with a future full of uncertainties. I shall endeavour to enlarge upon this statement at a later stage of my remarks.
May I now be permitted to deal more specifically with my own constituency of Kent, New Brunswick. The demographic situation of my county could not better be described than by the words of a friend of mine who, during a speech he made in the New Brunswick legislature a short time ago, had this to say:
In Kent county the population is 85 per cent French; the other 15 per cent is divided somewhat equally between the Irish, the English and the Scotch. We live together harmoniously and we are all liberals!
Before I endeavour to outline some special aspects of the conditions in my own constituency there is one point I want to clearly establish. I am outlining this picture in a purely objective manner without attempting at this time to apportion the responsibility for this situation to any existing authority particularly. Census reports from the 1951 census give us the following information with regard to the population of Kent county. During the ten years involved there were
8,000	births registered. During that same period of time 2,000 deaths were registered. Yet our net increase was but 1,000. It is therefore apparent that in those ten years

5.000	people, or about 83 per cent of the net natural increase, have left the county. Now, if we further analyse the situation we come to other undesirable conclusions. The majority of those leaving the county are those entering the earning period, that is to say our young people. In fact, in checking with the municipal officials, I received the information that during the year 1953 there were but 12 to 15 new homes built in the whole county-that is, in a county of some
27.000	population.
Under those conditions, it is therefore obvious that we are fast moving towards the status of a population composed mainly of children and old people. This in turn brings the unhappy situation where the increasing municipal burdens have to be borne by comparatively fewer people. In fact every year the school budget requirements are becoming heavier, due to an increasing demand for a more advanced teaching program. More schoolteachers have to be hired; new schools have to be built. Yet as soon as those who during their school age were a liability to the municipality reach the age where they should become an asset, they set out for other parts of the country, due to a lack of opportunities at home. The same situation now applies in our church organizations. In my own town of Buctouche we are just starting to build a new church. Due to the high number of large families, we have to build a large church. Naturally we would be very anxious, on the other hand, to keep most of that growing generation with us, when they attain the earning period, so that they could assume their part of the financial responsibility now contracted on account of them.
What is the answer to this situation? There is but one answer: To create opportunities. We are convinced that the greater number of those leaving the county are doing so through a matter of necessity and not through a matter of their own choice. We know that to be a fact, because when these people come back during vacation periods they tell us they would come back to stay if only they could make their living.
And how do we create new opportunities? May I suggest that a special study of the local conditions be made so as to determine every possibility to provide employment for our ever-increasing population. May I suggest, furthermore, that we need at least a few manufacturing industries in our county. While I know that in speaking that way, I may sound presumptuous, I do so for one reason that possibly very few others in this house, if any, could advance: Kent county is without a single permanent manufacturing 83276-275
The Budget-Mr. Michaud establishment. True, we have our fish plants along our shores, but these are only seasonal. For that reason I ask that the possibility of establishing any industry, be it of any size, be seriously investigated at the first opportunity. In the meantime I submit we should direct our attention towards a greater development of our primary industries, namely, agriculture, fishing and lumbering.
Agriculture, to me, always is an appealing subject. I imagine that when you are born on a farm, and brought up on a farm, it leaves impressions in your mind which will never fade. You can never forget those wide horizons, the charms and melodies of nature, the peaceful atmosphere of rural life. Nor can you forget the good people of the countryside, those rugged, hard-working farm men and women, who are the backbone of the country.
Mr. Speaker, let us be all solicitude for our country people; without them, our economy cannot be maintained. I have heard many true statements in this house about our farming people, and about the hard conditions they are facing. But I also feel that many things have been said in this house which contain something more than solicitude for the farmer's welfare; many a speech I have heard here, I submit, reflected more political display than economic dismay. Agriculture is a subject of major importance in our country, too important indeed to be abused for sheer political motives. Mankind has always subsisted through the land, and I contend that our Canadian way of life, depending to a large extent upon the prosperity of the farm, is not on the verge of disruption. When man will work the land diligently, yes in hardship at times, but also with hope, it will provide for him abundantly.
Mr. Speaker, it is well to accept those things which nature provides; but human ingenuity is also essential. Agriculture is the main industry of Kent county. Our farmers for the past few years have enjoyed certain advantages of great benefit to them; namely, the services of a devoted -class of agronomists, the benefits of the price and support board, the federal freight assistance, the helpful influence of the maritime co-operative services, free courses supplied by a school of agriculture, and others. Yet they also have their difficulties. The farmers of Kent county, like those in most part of the maritimes, are mixed farmers. The mixed farmers are probably those we hear the least about, although their difficulties are as great as those of any other class of farmers. Due to the small acreage of the Kent county farm there
4350	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Michaud remains little possibility of increasing the actual operations, which often fail to provide sufficient income to make it profitable. I would, therefore, be very anxious to see that an economic survey be conducted to ascertain the possibilities of improving the present conditions.
In that respect I am convinced that there are two fields of endeavour which, if carefully studied, could be very profitable to our farmers. First, I am sure that we are losing the opportunities of a profitable market in the canned vegetable and canned fruit business. I can think of no reason why we in the maritimes should look to the outside to supply our needs of those food commodities. Vegetables of almost every kind, and many varieties of fruits, grow well in our part of the country. And the vegetable crop arrives during vacation time, when the Children of our large families in Kent county could supply advantageously the necessary labour to pick those crops. And the high freight rates now existing in the transportation of goods would add to the advantages of such a project.
Secondly, I feel that for somewhat similar reasons we should be able in the maritimes to provide for our own requirements of canned milk. It was pointed out a few days ago by the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Murphy) that the design of the maritime industrial economy, in his own words, has suffered a decline since 1867. This situation, in some respects, has probably been brought about by an inferiority complex detrimental to our own welfare and prosperity. Why before perspectives like these should we meet only sentiments of doom, just because the initiative should start at home rather than somewhere abroad? In fact, a few experiments in some parts of the maritimes have already been made in these fields, and the results have proved very satisfactory.
A few years ago, in some sections of New Brunswick, no one had ever thought of making a great business of the strawberry crop. Today in those same areas this crop has become a thriving business, which brings good returns annually. Why could we not obtain the same results in other similar fields? These projects, canned vegetables, canned fruits, and canned milk, could be studied from a double angle. First, by subsidizing local firms or organizations willing to undertake such projects; or, secondly, by inviting firms already in those lines of business in other provinces to open branches in our own region. Such industries, I am sure, would be of great benefit to all in the


maritimes, to the farming population particularly, and in a special manner to my own farming population of Kent county.
Mr. Speaker, may I be permitted to say a few words about fisheries. The fishing industry in Kent county in the matter of importance comes next to agriculture. It will be easily understood, therefore, that I attach great importance to this subject. The people of the fishing villages of my constituency are hard-working people, striving to derive from their labours, sometimes with great risk, a modest subsistence. There are two observations I wish to make at this time, with regard to this industry.
First, I want to draw the attention of the government to the fact that I believe the time has now arrived when we should give more importance to education in the fishing industry. If I remember correctly, the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud) in his speech earlier made reference to the matter, and I concur in what he said. In agriculture, for instance, we have our technicians, our agronomists, our agricultural schools, our farm organizations. Our fishermen are also confronted with their problems, but have no institutions to assist in solving them. New regulations in the fishing industry are enacted every year. Most of the fishermen hear of these through government officials living in their midst, not as technicians ready to assist but as officers to enforce the law.
I believe if more stress was placed upon educating these people in the different aspects of their profession a lot of complications would be eliminated when law enforcement is applied. I am happy to say that an experiment of that nature will be attempted by the Department of Fisheries in Kent county shortly. I had requested that competent authorities be sent into the different fishing centres of the county to explain, in a series of educational talks, the numerous aspects of the lobster industry. This, I am informed, will be done before the next fishing season, and I am very happy about it. I hope that this initiative will be but a first step in a complete educational program for our fishermen everywhere.
I feel that in my own part of the province of New Brunswick, facilities for such a program could easily be obtained at St. Joseph's University. This institution, through the services of its extension division, has already proven to be of great assistance to our population, and I am sure the authorities would welcome the opportunity of further participation in the education of the fishing class of our population.

My second observation, sir, bears upon a subject of a particular nature: the oyster industry in Kent county. I can well remember when a very few years ago, this industry was very flourishing in my constituency. Today it has completely disappeared. And in the face of the present economic conditions of my county the importance of restoring this industry cannot be overemphasized. Our departmental technicians and scientists have the knowledge of the causes responsible for this condition. I now urge them to investigate the situation, and to use every means to revive the oyster industry in Kent county. We need it.
The third industry of Kent county is lumbering. Many depend upon it for their main source of livelihood, others as a supplement to their farm and fishing income. As a further result, this industry provides a substantial source of labour for the stevedoring industry during the navigation period, around the ports of Buctouche and Richibucto. The recent recession in the lumber industry has been felt in almost every business field of Kent county. It is hoped, therefore, that we will soon witness a return to those conditions when activity will again reign at its peak in our forests, along our roads, and around our ports for a better climate in the economy of Kent county.
I have no illusions, Mr. Speaker. The mandate I agreed to carry when elected to this house is heavy. I trust that with guidance and assistance all will be well.

It was with more than passing interest that I listened to the remarks of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) this afternoon. It rather seemed to me that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), having applied the lash a little while ago, the Prime Minister was now holding out the carrot, and that both of them, to a certain extent in their attitudes, seemed to feel the province of Quebec in its attitude was playing a little bit of the donkey. I for one cannot go along with that feeling. I do feel that we learned this afternoon there was going to be no federal-provincial conference in the immediate future. We learned that the Minister of Finance was not really being nasty in his remarks in the budget debate. He did not really slam the door. We did not learn very much else. It was unfortunate, first because we do very much need a conference between the provinces and the federal government at this point to resolve some of these difficulties, and we need it, Mr. Speaker, held in an atmosphere of amity, good understanding and 83276-275J
The Budget-Mr. Hamilton co-operation, and not in an atmosphere of mutual vilification, no matter how it is clothed.
We also need at such a conference to realize, all of us coming to that conference, that certain parts of this country have peculiarities that they are very proud of. The government, and particularly some of its luminaries, must realize this and approach the negotiations with the provinces of Canada with an understanding of the peculiarities and the differences of each region.
Quebec, Mr. Speaker, does not want to be set aside and treated as a region which is apart. We do have our regional differences perhaps; we have our prides and our peculiarities but I am an English Canadian coming from Quebec and that is why I am treating this subject in this way. Since I live in that province and meet the residents of that province day after day, so many of whom are French Canadians, I realize that they, their province, their philosophy and their thinking have made a tremendous contribution to the development of this country. Partially because of that and partially because of their own long history, they are jealous of their prerogatives.
They want the freedom to develop and to keep the traditions that they hold most dear. I hold no brief for those within Quebec who are isolationists and who would set the province apart. I hold no brief either for those here at Ottawa in this government who would set Quebec apart. I feel that perhaps the time has come when some of these things should be said, and when these regional differences and the necessity for operating within them should be recognized and should be emphasized.
I know as I go across this country, and I have been across it from one end to the other, that there are few people who realize just what is in the minds and in the hearts of most French-Canadian citizens in Quebec. They think of them as a people who perhaps want to live completely unto themselves. They do not realize that the French Canadian views himself as the first Canadian, as the one who is proudest, not only of his own little portion of Canada but of Canada as a whole. He views himself as having made, and as continuing to make, a tremendous contribution to the development of this country of ours. Within that framework, however, he does not feel that he should be anglicized or that he should have certain pressures exerted on him which would change his culture, that culture which has contributed so much to this country of
4352	HOUSE OF
The Budget*-Mr. Hamilton ours. Nor does he feel that he wants to impose his culture, his religion or his way of life or anything about him, upon the other parts of Canada.
He truly wants to live in amity with everyone. I think perhaps, Mr. Speaker-I hesitate to mention this-the change which those of us who live in Quebec can see in the attitude of those who live with us in the province towards international affairs bespeaks more than anything else the willingness of those in Quebec to learn to co-operate, and to change and fit themselves into the world as they know it. We do know that over the years the majority of the residents of our province have keenly felt the necessity for avoiding foreign wars or foreign entanglements. There have been many almost catastrophes that have occurred as a result of that feeling. Today, as our province becomes more urban, as the people of Quebec have learned more and have travelled more, the attitude of everyone in the province, French and English, toward international affairs has changed a great deal.
Just recently I read in the newspaper, for example, that the question of conscription, so long almost a fighting word in that province, was no longer a fighting word; that the people of Quebec were coming more and more to be prepared to play their part, as they have always done when the chips were actually down, in all phases of international affairs. I cite that, Mr. Speaker, and I do so perhaps using words very poorly, as some example of the thought I am trying to get across. It is a sincere desire on my part that this government should do more than simply say that the door is open. After all, doors are open under many circumstances, but people do not necessarily call at the door or go through the door unless they have reasonable assurance that on the other side they are going to be met with a welcome; they are going to be met with co-operation and kindness; they are going to be met by people who really want to sit down with them in amity and understanding to work out their problems.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that this government should give more indication than it has so far, not only that the door is open, but indicating the type of reception that will be found by those who go through that door. I believe that perhaps we have not as yet heard too much about that. Above all let us remember that while those in Quebec are particularly affected by this problem at this particular moment, it is a national problem that affects every province in Canada. It is going to affect us on a continuing basis until a reasonable solution is found. The evasion of the issue by not calling a federal-provincial conference is merely postponing the difficulty. rMr. Hamilton.]

May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker? At six o'clock the house took recess.

Mr. Speaker, when the house rose I had just concluded making a few remarks about the possibility of a federal-provincial conference. I would like now to turn my attention to the budget generally and express at least my personal regret at the general tone of the budget and my views on what it contains. I rather like to think of it as having been brought down by a likeable Minister of Finance who brought in an unlikeable budget. It is always the case that when unpleasant things are brought in by pleasant people we never know whether to discuss the unpleasantness of the thing or the pleasantness of the person. Actually this budget is one which seems to perpetuate the government's idea that a million dollars is just a drop in the budget and that decreases in the cost of one department must be balanced by increases in the amount allotted for another department.
There is one thing though we must say about our Minister of Finance and the government generally. They do not allow being rather hopelessly in debt to prevent them from spending. Certainly that must seem to be the case in view of some of the things included in the estimates. It does seem, however, Mr. Speaker, that we badly need a more careful study of the impact of taxation on the Canadian economy. The tax problem today is more difficult than it has ever been before in our history, and it is made so by problems of national security and by the high level of our social security payments. Since there seems to be general agreement that social security payments are necessary in the world of today, there are only two major fields in which reductions seem possible. One lies in the possibility of examining national security payments, and the second in administrative expenditures of all kinds. I think that perhaps in both these fields we have a great opportunity through increased efficiency and the elimination of waste and extravagance to reduce our expenditure quite considerably.
On the other hand, to allow national security expenditure to fall below the level necessary to provide a reasonable measure of national security would be absolutely foolhardy, and also to fail to levy ample taxes for national security and other government expenditure would really be self-defeating because in a time of full employment such

as this we would pay for these expenditures in another way which would, in effect, mean inflation.
We must work toward a solution of our tax problem by making progress in two directions. First, the development and execution of policies which will provide adequately for our national security at a minimum cost; and, secondly, the development of a tax system to meet the necessary costs of government, including the cost of national security, with the least impairment of national growth and the minimum of hindrance on the development of the individual in his work and in encouraging him to make the greatest possible contribution to our economy by providing him with sufficient monetary reward.
To give some idea of how our present tax structure penalizes the individual who makes an above the average income I have worked out comparisons on taxes paid over the lifetime of the statistically average Canadian, and two hypothetical individuals, the professional man and the medium successful businessman. Working from dominion bureau of statistics figures I have assumed that these men were married at the age of 27, which is the normal age for marriage in Canada, that they had their first child two years later, and the second child again two years later, so that you have here something approximating the average Canadian family.
The statistically average Canadian I have described here starts work at 16 and works until he is 70 years of age. It is interesting to note that his income by the time he is 27 years old and married is about $2,380 and then it rises to $2,558 from the period when he is 35 until he reaches the age of 44, and declines gradually from there on. However, throughout the lifetime of this statistically average Canadian-and this average is reached by taking the incomes of all Canadians and averaging them out-this individual never makes more than $50 per week, and on this he must establish a home, keep a wife, and raise two children as well as pay the government during the course of his lifetime the amount of $3,202 in income tax. For a man who never makes more than $50 per week this is an amazingly large sum. It is more than he will make in any one year of his lifetime, and it is more than he would require to put his son or daughter through college.
Then we turn to the businessman and the same set of figures apply. We estimate that he works from 17 to the age of 70 and that his income rises gradually from $2,000 to a top amount of $4,800 and then drops down ultimately as his earning power
The Budget-Mr. Hamilton declines to about $4,000. The Minister of Finance and his taxes, and the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) with his collections, will take from this man the sum of $21,715.
Then we turn to the professional man, the most highly paid class in Canada. I might add incidentally, Mr. Speaker, that in looking over these tabulations I was amused to find that as well as there being classes covering the professional men, salesmen, employed people and businessmen there was another class covering deceased. This made me realize just how extensive are the operations of the taxation departments.
These professional men start oft at the age of 25. Up to that time they have been obtaining an education. They start off with an average income of $3,000 and eventually their average reaches $7,400 and they finish work at the age of 65 making the sum of approximately $6,500 per year. Throughout the period of his lifetime, Mr. Speaker, this professional man pays the government $34,382 in income tax.
If hon. members will examine these figures for a moment they will see how tremendous is the burden which is being borne by the person who through his own efforts, initiative, or ability stands out above the ruck in any way, shape or form. The average Canadian pays the astonishing amount of $3,202 during his lifetime in income tax alone. The businessman on a medium income of approximately $5,000 a year pays $21,700, and the professional man with the average professional man's income pays $34,400.
We must remember there are men in every walk of life, in business, in factories, and men working with their hands in industry throughout this country who have the ability and even the desire to work a little harder in order to make a little bit more money to improve themselves. But with this tremendous impact of taxation on them as individuals, what incentive is there? It is bad enough when you examine it on the basis of one year; but when you examine it on the basis of a man's lifetime, you can see the reasons which might almost encourage him not to work so hard and not to make such a contribution to our economy when so much of it is going to be taken away from him in taxation.
I should now like to turn for a few moments to one other suggestion concerning the operation of business in Canada. The responsibilities of business and of industry in this country of ours are many; but perhaps the most important one of all is the responsibility of business and industry to improve

The Budget-Mr. Hamilton the living standard of everyone in Canada and to supply steady jobs for those who want to work. In order to accomplish this result, business and industry must constantly improve their present products, they must create new ones and they must persuade people to buy their output. In order to accomplish this objective there are certain methods and media which they can use.
Primarily, they have the work they can do on research on their products and on the improvement of those products. They have the work they can do in the field of research in finding new markets for themselves. They have the work they can do in the field of sales and advertising efforts to move these products into the hands of the consumer once they are manufactured. To me it seems that it is a primary responsibility of government to encourage business to operate in all these fields under all conditions, but particularly to offer business and industry some opportunity and some encouragement to operate in the fields of research and distribution of their products when times are difficult and when perhaps we are in a minor recession. At that time there is sometimes a tendency for business to restrict their expenditures or to cut back on expenditures which they feel can be carried over from one year to another. When sales slip, we must offer them the opportunity and the encouragement to carry on these important expenditures because it is essentially on them that our future prosperity is going to be based.
I suggest to the Minister of Finance that there might apply here something to which I referred last November in the course of the throne speech debate. I greatly regret not having seen something of that nature done when the budget was presented to us. To be specific, I am suggesting for his consideration that every business should be given the opportunity or the right to get a tax deduction each year, in addition to that which is now allowed, up to, say, 3 per cent of their sales dollar, in order that they might buy non-interest-bearing government bonds which would be redeemable at will by the buyer. The payment on these bonds would be allowed as a deductible expense. By the terms of this suggestion this money would have to be used either for research expenditures or for advertising expenditures. The buyer of the bonds could redeem them at will at any time. If he chose not to use the money for the designated purposes, he would be taxable on the amount at the time the bonds were redeemed. If he merely held the bonds for five years, they would be automatically redeemed at the end of the period and the buyer would be taxable on the


amount but he would not be taxed on that amount if he could prove that the amount of money redeemed through the bonds had been invested in research or in advertising. For research, he could use the money for the creation of new products, for new packaging or for new plant methods to produce products more cheaply. For advertising, he could use the money to stimulate the consumer into buying products through any means that were at his disposal.
The important thing is that the government of Canada would lose nothing through the introduction of such a measure because if the money was not used for the designated purposes the government would collect their taxes. If it was used for the designated purposes, there would be additional taxes coming to the government through increased business arising from the use of the money in this particular way and through increased employment which would result as the outcome of research into new products and the sale of those new products.
While this suggestion is perhaps new here, it is not really a new proposition. Something similar to this procedure has been done in Switzerland for some time. While it is a new proposition perhaps in exactly the way it is presented, we must remember that under our present tax laws, business and industry are allowed to do something quite similar in many fields. For example, through their accounting practice they can follow a procedure which moves profits from one year to another, and they can do this quite legitimately. Through inventory valuation they can accomplish the same thing. Through either capitalization or write-offs, at varying rates of their assets they can determine to an extent their taxation. Their depreciation policy generally has an effect on it. Of course, the major item is the carry-forward or carryback of losses in any one year in so far as they affect taxes. Under such a suggested procedure the government is, of course, in the position of getting rather considerable sums of interest-free money for anywhere from one to five years. I have already shown how the government would not lose in taxes collected under such procedure.
In conclusion, I put forward an idea such as this and I point out the heavy impact of taxation on the individual Canadian not in any hope or expectation that hon. members who sit opposite are going to be greatly impressed. I do it almost with a feeling that my words are falling on deaf ears. But it does seem to me we have got to realize at some point that, although it was the individual who built this country in the first instance, in the 1500's, 1600's and 1700's and, with an axe in

one hand and a gun in the other, pushed back our frontiers, although the industrialist and the businessman, that job having been done, have furthered that development in the last forty or fifty years and brought us to the rather comfortable position which we as individuals enjoy today, these incentives and opportunities are gradually being delimited and made smaller and smaller.
The man who thinks big in Canada today, under our government regulations, under government control, under government supervision, is at a disadvantage. In looking across the floor of the house I wonder how someone like the present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) would have felt if he had started out in life under the same restrictions, controls, taxation and everything else that his successors are encountering today. He is an older man now. He has made his mark, and certainly in the field of industry and engineering it is a good mark. But there are men who are going to come after him, men who are even now pushing themselves forward, who want to make a life here, a life that stands out, a life that means something, a life of accomplishment, who are not satisfied just to be another person, who are not satisfied to do another job but want to really accomplish something, and the incentive is being taken away from those people today.
Admittedly something else is being given in its place. They are being given cushions underneath them and all around them. They are being featherbedded, but the type of man I am talking about does not want featherbedding. He does not appreciate it. He appreciates the opportunity to live and do for himself and for his country to the best of his ability. I hope that in the years to come that type of man is going to be given the atmosphere in which to operate that will encourage him and lead him on. I do not think it ever will be done by the feather-bedders who sit opposite. It will be done by other groups, and primarily those among whom I sit, who have a keener appreciation of what built this country and made it great, and who can make this country greater than any member of the present government can even envisage.

speakeroldname: Mr. F. G. J. Hahn (New Westminster):
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are certain problems pertaining to the lower region of the Fraser valley and to British Columbia itself that have been well dealt with, such as the need for adequate diking and diking facilities, river crossings, provincial assistance and many others, and I do not intend to spend much more time on them. I wish to add my voice in endorsation
The Budget-Mr. Hahn of the stand taken by those who have raised them. We need dikes. Many people live in fear of our mighty Fraser river. We need means of crossing it, and there is a federal responsibility here. The Fraser is the St. Lawrence of British Columbia and we should regard it as such.
The fact that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has entered this debate is indicative of the need for a complete appraisal of the problems with which Canada finds itself faced today. Apparently the provinces are having financial difficulties. We have labour and unemployment problems. We have social assistance problems involving assistance to the aged, to the war veterans, to the blind and to the incapacitated. We have a problem of trade. We have a problem of conservation. The problem of taxation as it pertains to Quebec was dealt with to a degree by my associate, the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke (Mr. McLeod). I would also urge the government to be primarily concerned about the effect that the situation may have upon the morale of thousands of Canadians forced to live in the province of Quebec at the direction of the Department of National Defence. These include men and women in the armed forces and many civil servants who are not there of their own volition. Therefore particular consideration should be given them to see to it that they are not dealt with in this fashion. I was pleased that the Prime Minister agreed that some temporary agreement with the province of Quebec must be reached.
My main reason for taking part in the debate at this time is twofold. I wish to draw the attention of the government to a problem that is applicable particularly to my own riding and to the province of British Columbia as a whole but is also national in scope. I wish to deal with the question of fisheries and also the matter of our old age pensioners. With respect to the old age pensioners I have a part of table 23 here from the census of 1951 which deals with age distribution and gives the figures for those 70 years and over in the various provinces compared with the total population.
I have taken the time to figure out the percentage represented by those 70 years of age and over compared with the total population of the dominion. If I might be permitted at this time to have the table placed on Hansard I think I could save an appreciable amount of time.
