On a national basis those 70 years of age and over represent 4-7 per cent of our total population. The provinces in which the figure is greater than the national average are Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Ontario, Manitoba and British Columbia. The provinces in which the number of these 70 years of age and over is less than the national average are Newfoundland, Quebec, Alberta and Saskatchewan. The two provinces which are well above the national average are Prince Edward Island, with 6-5 per cent, and British Columbia with 6-3 per cent, compared with the national average of 4-7 per cent.
My own riding of New Westminster is well above these averages with 6 84 per cent of its population over 70 years of age. The population of the riding of New Westminster compares with that of the province of Prince Edward Island. The reason for people settling in these two regions, Prince Edward Island and the coastal region of British Columbia is, I find, primarily climatic, but many have also come to my riding on the specific advice of their physicians.
I am not going to deal with the emotional aspect of the problem of old age pensioners at this time. As the Prime Minister said, we must be realistic. As I see it, the problem is a realistic rather than an emotional one. The provinces of British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan have long realized the need of assisting these people.
Some years ago British Columbia supplemented the allowance of the aged by $10 a month. Alberta likewise had given their aged a supplementary allowance of $10 a month. So-called socialist Saskatchewan has


helped their aged to the extent of $2.50 a month. This year British Columbia and Alberta have each increased their assistance to $15 a month. Saskatchewan has undoubtedly found its cost of socialistic automobile insurance and health insurance will not permit it to increase its supplementary allowance, and so has added nothing to its supplementary allowance.
So we find that British Columbia gave $15 supplementary allowance per month, that Alberta gave a similar amount, and Saskatchewan $2.50. On the yearly basis the aged in British Columbia receive $180 supplementary allowance, those in Alberta receive the same amount and those in Saskatchewan $30. In the rest of Canada they receive nothing in addition to their regular old age pensions. But those persons eligible for old age pensions and supplementary allowance have a total income in Alberta and British Columbia of $480 plus $180 or $660, and in Saskatchewan $480 plus $30 or $510. In the other provinces of Canada they receive only $480.
Apparently, federally, we expect our aged to live on less than one-half the amount we allow by way of income tax exemptions for others. The problem resolves itself into four parts. First, there is the individual's ability to get and to hold a job. The individual must obtain a job and he must hold it if he intends to supplement his own allowance.
Secondly, there are municipal obligations -the ability to give medical and relief services to the individual. Then there is the provincial obligation-the recognition of its obligations to the individual and the municipality.
Fourth, we have the federal obligation, which includes the three-obligations to the province, the municipality and the individual. If we analyse each particular case we see this: In the individual we have as a society taken this man off the market as a labourer, and he therefore of necessity frequently becomes the responsibility of the state. We have declared him too old. He is a senior citizen. The municipality in such areas as Delta, Surrey, Langley and New Westminster, which I have the honour to represent, are hard pressed. They have many more than their comparative share of the senior citizens. The figures show that 6-8 per cent of their population are those of 70 years of age and over, while the rest of Canada has only 4-7 per cent. I might point out at this time that their average of 6-8 per cent is much higher than the rest of British Columbia, which is only 6-3 per cent; and that, in turn, is much higher than that of the rest of Canada. Many of them are not revenue producing. In the past they have not contributed to the cost

of operating the municipality, and they have not paid their share of the utilities costs. Many are ill and many are in need of medical help.
Then we find such municipalities as Surrey and Delta with no hospital facilities. They depend upon surrounding areas; they need and wish to build a hospital. They have in this particular instance tried for the last ten years to raise funds to do so, but have never been able to. The national health grant of $1,000 per bed is not sufficient to assist them, even though they have more than their share of the number of aged, as compared with the rest of Canada. They need help.
This poses the question: Is it the responsibility of the municipal district that has not received any revenue from some of its citizenry to supply them with this help; or is it a federal responsibility to try to help in these areas those who have come from other provinces? And therefore should not the federal government make a substantial contribution to those areas having considerably more than the Canadian average of aged? Certainly it would appear they are deserving of some help.
In British Columbia we find the average cost of hospitalizing senior citizens is $15 per month. Our municipalities should have a direct claim on each area which has sent us some of its senior citizens. You have most of the dividends of their labours. We have some of your finest citizens you have had.
The next obligation is provincial. I maintain that since British Columbia now gives a supplementary allowance of $15 per month to these people under a means test they have met their obligation. This is specially true when one adds the medical expenses of our senior citizens to this group. As I said earlier, it is at an average cost of $15 per month for old age pensioners.
Now I come to the federal responsibility. The major taxation field is in the hands of the federal authority. They give $40 per month. My proposal would be that the federal government should increase the old age pension to at least $60 per month. Where any man or woman is denied the privilege of working because he or she is too old, such persons should not be expected to live on less than $60 per month. That should be the minimum allowance from the federal government. It must be kept in mind that the senior citizen has only one alternative: He must choose food, clothing or shelter. Canada is a cold country, so he must pay the piper for a place to lay his head. That leaves him little with which to buy things to eat and to wear. The more he eats the less he wears; the more he wears the less he eats. Simple,
The Budget-Mr. Hahn isn't it? Let us try it some time-or perhaps the thirties give example enough. I appeal to hon. members to make this adjustment.
Earlier in the course of this debate the member for Okanagan-Revelstoke referred to the conservation of our forests in British Columbia, a problem to which we must give attention. Trees do not mature overnight. Reforestation is a problem of today, not of the distant future. It is the responsibility of this government to help protect the industry of the future. And I am sure every member in the house, be he Liberal, Conservative, C.C.F., Social Credit or an independent, will say, "We must protect Canada's forests". Therefore I shall not devote any more time to this problem. But as I said earlier: Conservation is one of those factors that require complete appraisal.
Frequently I feel the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) is right when he suggests that if the capital of Canada were much farther west we could expect different treatment from what we get today. I refer specifically to the apportionment of the tax dollar in direct relation to what our province contributes to the taxation coffers of the Minister of Finance.
I do not refer to the treatment from the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair). The people of my province for a time have had the utmost respect for his decisions. Up to now the Minister of Fisheries has given careful consideration to the fisheries problem in British Columbia. We now have a further problem of conservation, however, which has not received the careful study we think he should have given it. Therefore I am bringing the question of conservation of pink salmon on the Fraser river to his attention. We find there are three means of destruction of pink salmon, the first of which is the natural means, the second of which is man's stupidity and the third, fishing.
To deal first with the natural process of destruction. I would point out that this is the law of balance in nature whereby fish eat fish and birds eat fish and spawn, thereby gradually bringing about a balance through the process of survival. This, it seems to me, is self-explanatory.
The second means of destruction is that of man's stupidity. The erection of dams and other artificial impediments prevent fish going to their spawning ground. And we might add here the factor of the pollution of water about which we have heard so much in recent days. Quite frequently pollution destroys spawn and fish.

The Budget-Mr. Hahn
The third element of destruction is that of fishing. This is a process of deliberate destruction by man. I would say that the fisheries problem is a dual one.
I should like to point out what the province of British Columbia has done in the matter of the conservation of salmon. I shall read the report issued by the Fisheries Council of Canada on April 23 of this year, page 2, under the caption: "British Columbia bill to guard Salmon runs endorsed":
Vancouver Sun, April 9 reports: "Fisheries Minister Ralph Chetwynd in Victoria received a pat on the back for spear-heading provincial legislation to protect salmon from the river dam construction. Fisheries Association of British Columbia gave Chetwynd "full credit" for introducing Bill 47, an amendment to the fisheries act which received second reading in the legislature Wednesday. "The bill indicates the government does not intend to allow construction of hydro-electric installations at the expense of our valuable salmon fisheries", the association said. "This fact is implicit in the wording of the bill which clearly states the minister shall approve plans for a fishways, screens and other devices before construction starts." The association described Chetwynd as the "first provincial fisheries minister to fully recognize and accept responsibility which Victoria shares with Ottawa for protection of British Columbia resources against unilateral development."
Let us now go to the federal field. Here we have an announcement by our Minister of Fisheries that calls for the closure of the Fraser river above the Pattullo bridge after September 16 of each year. This affects the livelihood of some 600 fishermen, some parttime and some full-time. Now, Mr. Speaker, the fishermen on the Fraser river are aware of the need for conserving the British Columbia pink salmon run. 1 am sure our Minister of Fisheries will agree with that, but they are unhappy, very unhappy for very good reasons. The Department of Fisheries in its very democratic fashion sent a questionnaire to each fisherman and others interested in this business of conservation and related British Columbia fisheries problems of which closure of the river to fishing was question No. 5. To the best of our knowledge it is not proved by the majority report. If it is, then certainly the plea and resolution of the fishermen should be given more complete consideration.
I will therefore read a resolution of which I am sure the minister has a copy. I refer to the resolution issued by the United Fishermen and Allied Workers' Union, dated April 8, 1954, as follows:
Whereas the fisheries minister James Sinclair has officially stated that the Fraser river above Pattullo bridge will be closed each year after September 16, and
Whereas the two reasons given are conservation and quality, and
Whereas it can be shown that there is no difference in quality below or above the bridge and it does not offer a solution to conservation by closing that area but does, as a result, cause overcrowding

in other areas and creates extreme hardships to those fishermen who cannot move to other areas.
Therefore be it resolved that we use every means at our disposal to have the government rescind the closure above the Pattullo bridge.
Be it further resolved that we make a strong demand for the postponement of any final decision until 1956 in order to provide ample opportunity for full discussion with the fishermen directly affected, to give them ample opportunity to make adjustments, and to allow them to participate in the Adams river sockeye run in 1954.
Be it finally resolved we demand special compensation for the fishermen directly concerned by the federal government in event the department still insists on proceeding with the closure order.
I should like, Mr. Speaker, to deal with the preamble to this resolution. There is no question about the need of an explanation respecting the fact that the minister has called for closure of the fisheries. As far as the fishermen and I are concerned, the reason requiring the closure for conservation purposes meets with our approval. There is definite need for conservation of fish. As far as the quality of the fish is concerned, however, as you can discern from this resolution, up to now it has not been definitely ascertained that any man can go to the Fraser river and take samples of either fish that go up that river above or below the Pattullo bridge, and taste any difference in quality with any degree of accuracy. As far as the resolutions themselves are concerned I shall deal only with the one reading:
Be it finally resolved we demand special compensation for the fishermen directly concerned by the federal government . . .
In this particular case I would say that probably the fishermen concerned might have been much better advised to have requested the government rather than demanded that they do something about it. I am sure that a request would meet with more consideration. I would say that these are probably desperation tactics on the part of those particular individuals concerned.
On April 12 the United Fishermen and Allied Workers' Union-the same union to which I made reference a moment ago-had this to say in part II of a brief which I understand they have sent to the minister:
On February 5, 1954 the United Fishermen and Allied Workers' Union submitted a lengthy brief to the Department of Fisheries opposing this new regulation. We quote here from this brief: "The area above the Pattullo bridge accounted for less than 10 per cent of the sockeye, less than 3 per cent of the chums and less than 2 per cent of the cohoe, caught by Canadian fishermen in the Fraser river and its main approaches. Even in the Fraser river alone, area 29D (above Pattullo bridge) accounts for only 18 per cent of the sockeye, 16 per cent of the chums and 23 per cent of the cohoe. It is therefore clear that the elimination of fishing in this area is not vital to conservation of the salmon runs to the Fraser river. We might add that salmon fishing has been pursued in this area from the very beginning of the industry. We

do not believe it has suddenly become impossible to conserve our salmon, except by closing down this entire area.
We must also draw your attention to the fact that the date proposed for the closure of area 29D (above Pattullo bridge) coincides with the arrival of the Adams river sockeye run at the mouth of the Fraser. Thus, the fishermen who have been curtailed in their fishing efforts during the past eight years in order to rebuild the Fraser river sockeye runs would now be cut off. for all time, from any participation in these late runs of sockeye".
Mr. Speaker, reference to the documents that I have just read indicate that it is not a problem of conservation to deprive these men of fish that they have already conserved. They have a certain right to expect that they would have the privilege of fishing on these particular grounds. For the past eight years they have been protecting those grounds for the very purpose that they would have the right to fish when the fish began to run. Now that they are beginning to run they are being deprived of that particular privilege. I do not think that is quite playing cricket. I continue with the document:
The United Fishermen and Allied Workers' Union is absolutely opposed to the closure of the area between New Westminster and Mission bridge. We feel we should briefly sum up our objections as follows:
1.	Conservation of fall salmon, pinks and chums, or any other species of salmon, is not mainly dependent upon closure of this area.
That was indicated in the percentage of fish that was caught in that particular area, Mr. Speaker. I must say that I concur in the suggestion that the conservation of the fish is not dependent upon that area above the bridge. I continue:
2.	A treaty with the United States covering conservation of pink runs and equal catch division is the real need in conserving pink salmon and not the closure of any section of the Fraser.
You will probably recall that at the time of the throne speech I spoke along this same line and suggested that probably an agreement might be reached between the authorities in the United States and ourselves, particularly with the state of Washington, which is concerned, for the purpose of drawing up a commission similar to the sockeye commission to carry on the work of study of conservation. I understand that to a degree this commission is set up. I continue:
3.	Equalization of weekend closures between the approaches to the Fraser and the Fraser river combined with a deliberate program of equalizing catches between Canadian seiners and gillnetters would at the same time provide a better opportunity to apply conservation measures.
In respect to this suggestion that the fishermen themselves had to make, it appears to me that if the seiners and gillnetters are prepared to take off an extra day each week
The Budget-Mr. Hahn to permit the salmon to run up the Fraser, and therefore allow the fish to spawn, it would be a more reasonable excuse than to deprive 600 fishermen in the one section of the river from carrying on the fish trade that they have been used to doing for so many years. The brief continues:
4.	Overcrowding in the industry must be solved by a fair program of licence limitation, not by eliminating our historic fishing grounds.
I would not completely agree with this idea of licence limitation. The very fact that we are living in a world of free enterprise would, in itself, indicate that each person should be privileged to enjoy fishing in an area where others are permitted to do so for commercial purposes. However, since we are limiting the number of fish that we are allowing these people to catch, there may be a certain justification in permitting our government to issue licences to them.
Now, there is one other suggestion that I would add to this group respecting licences in those fields, and it is this. In the event of licensing, and in the event that the minister feels we are going to have to close the river, then I would suggest that the government should grant these licences and make them revocable on a basis of possibly ten or fifteen per year, as the case might be, and provide these fishermen with another means whereby they can earn their livelihood. One must understand the situation thoroughly. One must realize that the Pattullo bridge in this instance divides the Fraser at the city of New Westminster. About half of the gill netters work on the east side of the Pattullo bridge and the other half on the west side. What is being suggested is that the group shall move from the eastern side of the bridge, about six hundred of them, down into the western side of the bridge where there is a larger body of water. However, by not stopping these fishermen from fishing in that area west of the bridge I maintain, and so do the fishermen, that we are just transplanting the problem. We are not going to solve the problem of conservation. We are still going to have to tell these people they can only fish so many days each week.
I believe that the Department of Fisheries, and the capable minister, realizes that since the Fraser river channel is becoming one of the continent's most rapidly growing fresh water navigation centres, we should at least be prepared to stop fishing in that area at some time. I know that the fishermen in that area fully realize the necessity for cutting down on fishing licences, but they are not prepared to go along at this time with the sudden request that the fisheries shall close on September 16. I am quite aware of the fact that this thing has been growing for

The Budget-Mr. Lusby years. I do know that the fishermen, too, had 'been aware of that fact to a degree, but they had not been told at any time that this was the year so that they might have prepared themselves for it. It is for that reason they are making the request that an extension be granted this year and possibly to 1956, which would give them the chance to reestablish themselves in other occupations.
As I said earlier, some of them are not fully occupied in the fishing industry, but they supplement their income by fishing. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) knows how difficult he would find things if they gave him another 600 unemployed and said, "Here, you have to find jobs for them". It would make him quite unhappy, and I would sooner see a group of fishermen partly unhappy than see our Minister of Labour completely sad. I, therefore, request that the Minister of Fisheries and this government reconsider the announcement of the closure of the fisheries on the Fraser river after September 16 each year, and deal with the problem in the manner it has been my privilege to propose.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
As we
reach the later stages of this budget debate, I have no desire to prolong its life unduly. I should like, however, to take the opportunity to make some comments with regard, not only to the budget itself but also to certain matters of public interest with which this or any budget necessarily has a definite connection. I think also, Mr. Speaker, I shall take just one moment to extend to my colleague and office mate the hon. member

for Kent, N.B. (Mr. Michaud), who apparently has been promoted to the cabinet, my congratulations upon his excellent maiden speech delivered in this chamber this afternoon.
Like many other citizens I have in the past followed with some degree of attention, through the medium of the press and the radio, the annual presentation of the budget. The presentation of this budget is, of course, the first one that has been accompanied- I will not say adorned-by my presence on the floor of this house, an effective guarantee of my keener interest. I suppose, therefore, that I may still fairly call myself, to an appreciable extent at least, a budget neophyte. The word, I think, in addition to its meaning as a novice or a tyro, may also designate a convert or new believer. I find that on the present occasion, and with reference to myself, I may safely use it in both senses. It is my firm opinion that this budget is a sound and equitable one, a budget suited to the times. In his presentation of it on April 6, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) has given to the Canadian people, whom it so immediately affects, a budget statement which they have found both acceptable and, for the most part at least, reassuring.
Viewed merely as, shall we say, an extended communique from the taxation battlefront, or a recurring tally of what is required of our citizens in the way of rendering unto Caesar the things that are Caesar's, the budget forms a financial document of exceeding importance. But in a broader sense, seen as a mirror of our entire national and economic life, our external relations in a troubled world and our prospects for the future, the budget and its presentation go far beyond mere finance and become a matter of vital concern to all Canadians. That, I take it, is the major reason for the wide latitude of topics traditionally allowed in this debate.
During the last few months much has been said, both within and beyond the confines of this chamber, concerning the perils, the difficulties, the problems which menace our national safety, our democratic freedom and our diversified economy. In the spate of discussion there has been, to my mind, a very real distortion of emphasis, in the economic field at least, by the opponents of this government. Marked stress has been laid upon the darker aspects of the picture, but there has been a tendency to underrate or ignore the existence of those favouring factors which can operate so powerfully as a redressing influence. In my opinion, the minister's budget speech has contributed notably to restoring a saner perspective.
It is true that in that vast and often obscure sphere of international relations,

wherein lie ultimate peace or war, there cannot as yet be any high degree of optimism, nor did the minister attempt to exhibit it. Even here, of course, there are favouring factors. But for all the increase in armed strength of the west, for all the earnest if groping efforts towards attainment of lasting settlements, no responsible person can seriously argue that the shadow of a third world conflict does not still hang dark above us, an ominous and constant threat to our security and very existence. And until that shadow departs and a stable peace is assured the cost of our national defence must inevitably continue as by far the largest single classification of government expenditure. Even success in the current negotiations at Geneva can achieve only a troubled peace, permitting no relaxation of vigilance. To drowse at any time beside the bear and the dragon would be to court a rude awakening.
To all considerations of peace and war there has been imparted an urgency, as of desperation, by the recent revelations of the stupendous powers of mass destruction now available to man in the hydrogen bomb. To many the results of the Pacific tests have meant literally the end of all hope, and a descent toward either inertia or hysteria.
The minds and souls of men recoil in horror from the grim potentialities of the future. And yet here too there has been, I think understandably enough, a distortion, a confusion in popular thought, between the dangers which total war would bring and the danger of its occurring. The imminence of the latter has tended to be confused with the magnitude of the former.
But that greatest of statesmen, that rarely fallible prophet of the international scene, Sir Winston Churchill, has made a calmer appraisal. To him the hydrogen bomb has in fact lessened, rather than augmented, the likelihood of a third war of the great powers. Apart altogether from the stature of the British Prime Minister, his reasoning appeals to many, among whom I count myself. What man, or group of men, would deliberately invoke a world conflict when the price and fruits of victory have so terrible an identity with the penalties of defeat?
That is not to say that the hydrogen bomb is or ever can be a guarantee of peace. Great wars have been precipitated in the past, and may be again, by the accident of events, with scant deliberation or forethought on either side. And the hydrogen bomb may even increase the incidence of perimeter wars such as we know in Korea and Indo-China. For the communist world, shrinking, even as we do, from the consequences of a direct clash
The Budget-Mr. Lushy between the great powers, may well divert an increasing segment of its strength towards the fomenting of such acts of aggression as may, with little likelihood of H-bomb reprisal, sweep one by one the lands of Asia, of the Middle East, and of Africa into its pouch. That is a mounting danger, not to be effectively met or averted by any threat of the hydrogen bomb, which, in the circumstances, as our enemies could well foresee and count upon, would almost certainly never be translated into action. And yet we must be resolute and able to act against any such aggression. We know that if, by gradual encroachment elsewhere, the free west is reduced to the status of a beleaguered fortress, a larger Dien Bien Phu in a uniformly hostile world, the ultimate fall of that fortress is inevitable.
Is it not apparent then that to guard against and, if necessary, to resist and repel all or any such aggressions wherever they may occur, the democracies must maintain their armed strength at the highest level in every conventional form as the only means for effective action?
And again, even in a major conflict, one cannot entirely ignore the possibility that the horrors of the hydrogen bomb may impel a mutual abstention from its use. And finally, even if these bombs fall, many experts of war still envisage a real and vital role, both in defence and in attack, for the fighting forces of land and sea and air which have constituted our bulwarks of the immediate past.
To me, therefore, the suggestion that such existing forces, with their conventional weapons, are obsolete, their maintenance and expansion a needless and wasteful drain upon this country's economy, has no foundation in either present reality or future probability. It could be justified only by the achievement of a just, enduring, and universal peace, and that is still far from us, not yet engendered in the minds of men.
Not only this year, therefore, but indefinitely we must continue to provide for our national defence those vast sums which represent so great a part of our entire governmental revenue. No budget can be compiled, no plan laid for the expansion of the national economy or the advancement of our people, without taking into full account that formidable necessity. Certain critics of the present budget might well bear this more clearly in mind.
I turn to our economic situation concerning which, as I have said, I see an undue distortion toward gloom in the professed thinking of many opposition members in this house. As a corollary, they have inevitably accused the Minister of Finance of unwarranted

The Budget-Mr. Lusby optimism in his budgetary conclusions. This is not, by many, the first year in which his critics have laid that charge at his door. Thus they have been hammering at him, like woodpeckers against armour plate, for the best part of a decade. But he has confounded those critics uniformly and often -nine times, the count, is it not? And it is my prediction that the present occasion will constitute the tenth. They may, however, draw some consolation from the thought that thereafter their humiliation, that is at the hands of this particular Minister of Finance, seems likely to end.
As I have indicated, I hold the minister's outlook for our economic future to be amply justified. Indeed, there are already signs that the earlier government forecasts of an upward trend in business as the year rolled on are to prove accurate. And considering the position of Canada, the vast possibilities for development within her borders, the wealth of her natural resources, and the character of her people, I see little room to doubt that her history for many years to come, given only peace, will be one of advancement and prosperity.
That is not to say, Mr. Speaker, that our progress will be without minor, sometimes perhaps substantial, interruptions and setbacks. One must never forget that dependent as we are on foreign trade to dispose of much of what we produce we are far from being complete masters of our own commercial destiny.
I do not wish to imply by anything I have said that I am in a mood of unreflecting optimism. Indeed it would be difficult for one from the maritimes to be ever wholly optimistic concerning the economic future of those provinces, for our special economic problems we have always with us, to a greater degree, I think, than any other area of Canada.
Not long ago, Mr. Speaker, another and veteran member of this house, from a different part of the country, remarked to me that the present session had seen less talk than usual concerning maritime rights. The truth of this statement my brief experience cannot gauge. But if there has been in fact during this session less assertion of maritime rights, or aspirations, or difficulties, I can assure the house that it is not because of lack of material. So long as geography leaves us where we are-and I see no prospect of any imminent change in that regard-we shall remain a distinct regional entity with problems and difficulties uniquely our own.
This brings me to a point on which I wish to lay particular emphasis. Laissez-faire is dead. The evolution of democratic


government has long been toward assuming a steadily widening responsibility for the economic welfare of nations and people. It is a process, I think, not only advantageous but inevitable. That is not to say, of course, that this or any other government is or can be a complete underwriter of prosperity. Business and industry, as in the past, must stand primarily by their own efforts. But few now question that it is an accepted function and duty of this government to foster and encourage, to every reasonable extent, those economic conditions under which business and industry may best flourish and our people correspondingly benefit.
Now, it is my contention, Mr. Speaker, that this responsibility is not discharged in its entirety if, whatever the opulence of the country as a whole, the prosperity of any one region lags unduly behind that of the rest. In such case, I hold it to be the peculiar obligation of the national government to alleviate by every reasonable exercise of its legitimate powers the effect of those handicaps, geographical or otherwise, which militate against that region's economy.
Any dream of a universal equality, or near equality, of prosperity throughout the nation must I fear remain a dream; but every region is entitled to a fair place in the economic sun, and the lessening of existing discrepancies should at all times form a prime objective of this government.
The maritime provinces, unfortunately, have almost traditionally lagged behind the rest of Canada in the economic race. Like the other parts of the country, we have made material progress in recent years, but we are still, relatively as well as absolutely, far in the rear. The grossness of existing inequalities calls for strong remedial action toward their abatement.
I am happy to say that this government is not unmindful of its obligations in this regard, and that many measures which it has inaugurated have contributed substantially to the advancement of the maritimes.
This has been true to a degree even in fields where no special regional significance is evident or intended. The great achievements of social security, old age and family allowances, unemployment insurance, and veterans benefits have no merely regional application; and yet I think that, relatively speaking, they benefit most those provinces whose people have least. So indeed it is with every federal measure involving proportional expenditures throughout the whole country.
Other federal action has been aimed directly, and with a fair degree of success, at stimulating our maritime economy. In

the field of freight rates, where so many of our commercial ills originate, much has been done by way of alleviation. The system of coal subventions and the assisted movement of feed grains from west to east have all played their part and have earned for this government the trust which our people have accorded it. Yet the task remains heavy if the maritimes are to enjoy their full and rightful share of the national prosperity. It is not, I think, primarily a matter of doing now what should have been done in the past, although I shall cite one or two instances of that nature. Rather, there is a need to devise new measures or to expand existing measures in order to overcome new problems as they arise; and of newly-arisen problems the economic history of the maritimes has always shown a plenitude.
Of all the sweeping changes which have affected the economy of this country since confederation few, whatever the ultimate good, have failed to come initially as a staggering blow to the maritimes. We may go back to that vast sea shift from sail to steam in the last century which ended their golden age. We may come forward to this very hour and find the Nova Scotia coal industry, a chief prop of the economic life of the province, facing a desperate struggle for survival against the increasing competition of oil and gas from the new fields of western Canada. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, the obligations of this government towards the maritimes can never be regarded as static. They go far beyond the mere continuation of existing measures which now may well prove to be inadequate. Such new action must be taken and such new measures must be devised as will prove at least sufficient to prevent any further deterioration of our maritime economy as compared with that of the rest of Canada. I am, of course, well aware that the problem is not that of the federal government alone. Each province concerned has its own responsibility-and an urgent one-to shoulder. Of my own province I may say that it faces the task with energy and determination.
But here I must point out an inherent evil in the situation. Lack of economic development and opportunity creates the need for action. The same lack inevitably limits the provincial capacity to meet the need. The financial resources of the maritime governments are slight compared with those available to the governments of the wealthier and more populous provinces where, at the same time, the problem of economic expansion virtually solves itself. Thus it is that
The Budget-Mr. Lusby the greater the burden, the less the provincial capacity to sustain it. In our maritime provinces we must therefore look-and I maintain that we have the right to do so- to this federal government for a correspondingly generous measure of assistance in the removal of those barriers which so greatly beset our path of economic progress. The enduring prosperity of this nation demands the prosperity of all its parts. Let none forget that we too were created the heirs of Canada.
In what forms should such assistance be devised and extended? To a lame man a crutch may be desirable or necessary, but a lasting cure of his affliction is much to be preferred. Therefore the real aim for the maritimes-certainly not always to be easily achieved-should be the permanent strengthening of their economy in all its phases, including farming, mining, lumbering, fishing and manufacturing. No other benefits within the power of this government to bestow- whether of social security or otherwise-can begin to match the benefits that would flow from the attainment of this aim. I have mentioned the advantages of social security measures to the maritimes, but I think perhaps I should also say that we certainly have no wish to be reduced to the status of a race of pensioners.
The most immediate of our problems in Nova Scotia is that of the coal industry. However, since this industry will no doubt be the subject of extended debate in connection with the dominion coal board estimates, I touch upon it at present no further than to say that the preservation of this industry is essential to the provincial economy, and that there exists a reasonable prospect that adequate governmental assistance now will enable it not only to survive but to stand again largely upon its own feet within the next decade.
Perhaps I should interpolate here that I accept as sound the view that no government can or should adopt a policy of perpetual assistance to every industry which, without that assistance, cannot continue to operate. No government can entirely repeal the law that an industry must be able to meet competition or give way to those that can. On the other hand, it has long been recognized in this country-and I think it is not seriously disputed-that a policy of governmental assistance to certain key industries on which a national or regional economy depends is often not only desirable but imperative. Every case must be judged on its individual merits. On that ground I am confident that the maritime coal industry has the strongest

The Budget-Mr. Bushy of claims upon this government, as will be fully demonstrated, I hope, when they are presented in this house on the fitting occasion.
As I said a few moments ago, maintaining our maritime economic life at a respectable level, in so far as this government is concerned, is not merely a matter of continuing measures which may have sufficed in the past. The inevitability of change prohibits a static policy. Let us then consider possible new measures to stimulate maritime economic activity and to prevent the occurrence of any undue unemployment. I stated earlier that this nation faces the necessity, extending into an indefinite future, of maintaining a towering level of expenditure for armed defence. Thus governmental contracts in this connection will continue to play a leading part on the industrial scene.
I think much can he said for the view that in the placing of such contracts very special consideration should be given, as a matter of national policy, to those areas which, like the maritimes, stand most in need of industrial stimulation. It might be added that such a policy would also tend to discourage the overexpansion of certain already established industries of central Canada. We have been told that such overexpansion is a major cause of the difficulties troubling some of those industries today.
Whenever the need arises to quicken industrial activity and to provide increased employment a vast program of public works is invariably suggested. Public works are an excellent thing, and I should be delighted to learn, for example, that a new post office was on the drafting board for every hamlet in my constituency. Undoubtedly a considerable amount of employment would be thereby created. Unfortunately, it would be for the most part of a temporary nature and merely a palliative. Our situation in the maritimes calls rather for more lasting remedies through a permanent development and expansion of our industrial and other economic activities.
Again, it has been pointed out that in this day of power machinery the number of men employed, even on extensive public works, is as a rule comparatively small. In this connection, however, I should like to emphasize a difference between two classes of public works. Incidentally, may I say that I am using the term "public works" in a very broad sense, and not merely as referring to projects properly coming within the scope of the department of that name so ably presided over by my fellow Nova Scotian, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters). One class might be exemplified by new post offices or, indeed, by most new government buildings.


This class of public work provides a certain amount of employment during its construction. Upon completion it may, and usually does, fill a long-felt need and minister to the pride and convenience of local residents. But there its contribution to the economy of a community or the surrounding areas largely ends.
On the other hand, we have that type of public work which, in addition to achieving all these results, also exerts a lasting and beneficent effect upon the level of economic activity throughout a community or a whole region. That is, to my mind, the type of public work which, when proposed, should always receive from this government the most careful and sympathetic consideration, the more so when the objective is the permanent advancement of areas such as the maritimes. Any temporary abatement of unemployment to be afforded by the actual construction-desirable though it might be in itself-would constitute only a minor factor in the whole range of implications.
An outstanding instance of this type of public work is the proposed St. Lawrence seaway development. Nova Scotia also is not without examples. The marshland reclamation now being carried on there and elsewhere is one. Its benefits to the segment of our agricultural population affected are for the generations, although I suggest-as I have suggested before-that the full and rounded completion of the project involves also a vastly expanded program of research to determine all those potential new uses to which the reclaimed lands may be most profitably put.
If I may call it a public work within my broad definition, then I may also name the Yarmouth-Bar Harbor ferry soon to be in operation and so largely a result of the forward vision and indomitable persistence of my good friend, the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare (Mr. Kirk). The stimulus which this ferry will give to our growing tourist trade, as well as to the general commercial life of western Nova Scotia, is incalculable.
To the people of my own immediate area, however, the Chignecto canal will remain the prototype of the class of public work I have last mentioned. We do not urge construction of the canal merely because of the employment to be created by its building, or merely because it represents an unfulfilled promise of confederation. We urge it rather because of the permanent and far-reaching uplift which we are confident it will bring to the economic life of the whole territory of the maritimes, as well as to Newfoundland and even farther afield.

The employment of a few hundred men for perhaps two or three years upon the actual construction would be indeed welcome, and nowhere more than in my own town of Amherst which stands almost upon the canal's prospective banks; but that result, that benefit, is of scant significance compared with the comprehensive and lasting advantages to our economy which the canal and its use will bring.
The hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Murphy) recently gave a detailed and convincing account of these latter advantages which, indeed, anyone can substantiate by glancing at a map. The hon. member for Colchester-Hants (Mr. Purdy) has also touched upon the topic. I have no wish to repeat or elaborate further at this time upon what they have said, but I certainly add to it my hearty concurrence. If this government seeks ways and means for the permanent strengthening of our maritime economy, here is a beckoning opportunity.
And, indeed, my constituency provides another, if less spectacular, opportunity. For many years until the last war, when its operation was discontinued, an automobilecarrying ferry, subsidized by the federal government, plied between the port of Parrsboro on the Minas basin shore of my constituency and ports of Kings county on the opposite side of the basin. By this means a water route of some fifteen or twenty miles eliminated for motor vehicle traffic an overland journey of ten times the distance along the shores of Minas basin and Cobequid bay to Truro, which stands at the head of salt water, and thence down the far shores again.
Apart altogether from the convenience to local residents, the ferry was much patronized by tourists, and today, with the vastly increased stream of tourist traffic, it would be put to correspondingly greater use and would give a very strong impetus to that trade which is to us a major source of revenue. I hope to see in the not distant future comprehensive representations made to the government for assistance in effecting a resumption of this ferry service with expanded and improved facilities. I most earnestly hope that these representations, when they are made, will be given most careful study and most sympathetic consideration.
Turning to another topic, I may say that we of the maritimes heartily approve the steps taken by the government, in conjunction with those of the provinces, to widen the scope of the vocational training program so that persons displaced from one industry may be trained for employment in others. This will certainly prove a boon in countless
The Budget-Mr. Small individual cases, and as such it deserves the highest commendation. But the advantage to a province as such is dependent chiefly upon there being within that province alternative industries capable of absorbing the retrained workers. From a maritime point of view, the placing of those workers in the industries of central Canada, however beneficial it will be for the individuals concerned, represents a loss to us. And so we return to our fundamental need, a general stimulation and expansion of all phases of our economy.
It has been predicted-I am going into the future now-that the continuing threat of war may eventually lead, as a measure of national safety, to the widespread dispersal throughout all the provinces of those manufacturing industries now so heavily concentrated in central Canada. By such an occurrence the maritimes would presumably benefit in their degree. But for the present it is no more than a possibility of the future.
Equally of the future is the suggestion that the coming application of atomic power to industrial use may accomplish somewhat the same result and bring all provincial economies more nearly to a common and equitable level. As to that, we shall see. An easier prediction, I fear, is that the misuse of the atom in war may bring all mankind to a common level, the illimitable level of the desert. For the meantime it is better to deal with present realities and for us in the maritimes to face as they are those economic problems which still beset us. With the full co-operation of this government, given to us in the future as it has been in the past, they can be overcome.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, having listened to the budget debate, with all the fanfare attending it, from the beginning, and the different titles that have been given to it, and having witnessed the debonair manner in which the finance minister delivered his budget speech, I think it was a masterly job of making the best out of the sorry mess the government is in. First everything is lovely and we will be all right, but there are one or two soft spots. We will have an odd rough one here or there. The industries are doing fine, except for textiles, machinery and electrical equipment. The farmers are not doing as well as usual. In other words, we are going to have a good year if we do not run into the hard times that I see ahead and that I hope we can miss.
You could call this budget the much ado about nothing budget. At page 3724 of

The Budget-Mr. Small Hansard of April 6, 1954, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) said in his budget address:
For most of this period the United States has been in the process of re-examining its . . . policies. . .
He went on to say that the United States commission on foreign economic policy had issued its report, the Randall report, and then said that the recommendations contained in the report-
. . . provide ... a reasonably promising basis for action by the United States in a co-operative movement toward a sounder system of trade and payments.
I suppose this reasonably sound basis in a co-operative movement is to be found in the restrictions by way of quota that they have imposed on our rye shipments to them and the inhibitions that our cattle trade endures which I presume come under the broad and expansive application of the GATT program, that instrument of vague benefit to Canada since it has been in operation and which has therefore been extended to June 30, 1955. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) also said:
The United States has been one of the strongest exponents of policies directed towards the reduction of trade barriers and the expansion of international trade.
So much is this so that they have contributed to the deterioration and demise of our textile industry, and they play havoc with our fruit, vegetable and flower markets in the springtime. This was further ameliorated by the Minister of Finance in these consoling words:
... it was recognized that enlightened economic policies on the part of both the United States and Canada would contribute materially to the achievement of a better trade . . . system throughout the free world ... To this end the United States administration has just placed before congress a program designed to give effect to the main recommendations of the Randall commission.
I suppose that the government is confident that these recommendations will be passed by the House of Representatives and the Senate in toto. The Minister of Finance also stated, as found on page 3724 of Hansard:
As might be expected, this development has brought with it growing protectionist pressures in many countries, including Canada.
What could he expect? Why, all through the debate on the speech from the throne and in subsequent debates there was a constant litany from the government seats, the epitome of which was "from this, good Lord, deliver us, and give protection to relieve our local condition."
The cool merger of free traders with the protectionists on the government benches insisting that something be done about the

withering condition of trade is causing an increase in unemployment in every walk of life in our economy. They pictured the difficulties of the farmer, the fisherman, the potato grower, the textile worker, the lumberman, the apple grower, the miner, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and implored that something be done to give some kind of relief from the business atrophy that has beset us since the last election when Canada's continued prosperity was promised, when the assorted aggregation of "pie-in-the-sky" boys who grace the benches opposite were masquerading as the evangels of everlasting prosperity with the proverbial pot of gold at the end of the rainbow, which has turned out to be only dross, in the form of unemployment, loss of markets, and adverse trade balances. Well, the warning signals are now flying to tell of stormy weather ahead. Whether or not it is palatable to this so-called "free trade" government, they tell that we will have to protect the home markets and industries.
The traditional policy of the Conservative party has been the development of our natural resources and their fabrication into consumer goods, as well as the protection of our labour potential, and we have always implemented this by legislation brought in by the front door; but the Liberals have always brought it in by the back door, and masquerade as free traders under a cloak of simulated protection. It is the voice of Jacob but the hand of Esau. The Minister of Finance also states:
Our very large defence program continued to give strong support to production and personal incomes, but this element has become a sustaining rather than an expansionist force.
There is the nub of the whole situation today around which our economy is wrapped, and the levelling off process is the sequence that has stabilized our economy and kept it from disintegrating. But in its wake has followed a plethora of financial organizations that are ever ready to lend the hard-pressed citizen, who is now feeling the pinch of the government's alluring policies, needed money at high rates of interest to see them through Canada's continued prosperity. Then he gives this fillip to their flagging spirits, to encourage them:
-while the proportion of our exports going to the United Kingdom and other commonwealth markets declined, reversing the trend, which had prevailed during 1952.
On the other hand, there was some increase in the proportion of our imports coming from the United Kingdom.
You will notice the hedging in the last sentence of this quotation, to explain the lost wheat market.

43G7
That hackneyed phrase, "no truck or trade with the Yankees", seems to be a favourite expression of accusation of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) in his tirades against the Conservatives. Well, it is obvious now that, intentionally or not, there has been put into operation by the government, to our detriment, a quite opposite policy: "No truck or trade with the British", and they are enjoying with evident satisfaction that accomplishment, little realizing that they have impaired the flow of the lifeblood of our nation. He further states:
The emergence of an Import surplus on merchandise account was the main reason for the swing in Canada's balance of payments position from a current account surplus of $157 million in 1952 to a deficit of some $467 million in 1953.
Reduced to ordinary language, we had more imports than exports by some $310 million. That can be attributed to our two jacks of trade, the right and left bowers, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), who have trumped each other's ace-or probably we can call it a misdeal- in their handling of our wheat crop. One said sell, the other said hold, and between the two the farmers were left holding the bag.
The only satisfaction that the wheat growers have extracted out of it is that the Minister of Trade and Commerce has restored to them as of December last the car order book to take a few paltry bushels per acre to the storage elevators, while the advice of the Minister of Agriculture was ignored; the double shuffle took place, and the deal lost us the British market for a difference of eight cents a bushel, and a difference of $150 million surplus to $460 million deficit, with the farmers rich in the possession of wheat they cannot sell, the farm implement industry on short rations, the shipping industry folded up, and the railways on the skids to deficit earnings. What one hell of a mess in continuing Canada's prosperity!
We on this continent are living in a paradise, with our country unscathed by the hand of war. We have a standard of living that three-quarters of the world's human population have never enjoyed, and if they have any knowledge of it, it is from the picture and story books.
For the last decade and a half, the total productivity of our economy was in demand, and that demand far exceeded our ability to supply. There were ready markets for our goods, both abroad and at home. With the cessation of the war, and our armed forces repatriated, there was a huge backlog for all kinds of durable goods to be supplied, caused by the shortage of materials necessary for our wartime economy-houses to
The Budget-Mr. Small be built-homes to be furnished-clothes to refurbish the depleted wardrobes-plus the expansion in our industry, and the need for getting the war-wracked and devastated countries back on the road to recovery.
That we have flourished and prospered was not the creation or design of this government, who could neither retard nor accelerate it. It can be attributed to the productivity of labour and management, who have been rewarded for a job well done by the government letting inflation run rampant; the bonds and securities purchased in good faith are worth but half in their purchasing value, and the purchasing power of our dollar is only fifty cents, and probably less after we have paid our taxes.
Today, with our inflated economy, which the government created, we have barriers to our entry into world markets, and this is further aggravated by the re-entry into world trade of Germany, Japan, Italy and the other war-devastated countries, and the reluctance of the Latin-American countries to deal with us, notwithstanding the glowing reports from the Minister of Trade and Commerce after his visit to them.
In Hansard of February 17, 1954, page 2189, the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Philpott), speaking in the unemployment debate, was discussing the last worldwide depression of the 1930's, and he said:
I think there Is a lot in this theory of the stars, astrology, or whatever It may be. 1 do not know whether the Conservatives turn up before a depression, or whether the depression turns up before the Conservatives, but you find they arrive at almost the same time, in this country.
Well, the stars in their courses may indicate that a certain condition will happen in the cycles of life. I will tell the hon. member for Vancouver South that his conclusions are at fault. It is not that the depression and Conservatives arrive together. The truth of the matter is that the Liberals, when in power, eventually get the country into such an unholy mess that the people turn to the Conservatives to extricate them from their plight, and again bring about stabilization and the consolidation of our economy. And that day is not far off.
The Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Lesage) made reference in Hansard of April 14 to an adherence to the spirit of confederation to establish an equality of treatment in the distribution of revenues to all provinces, so that they may fulfil their constitutional obligations, and effect fiscal agreements that would avoid double taxation. To this everyone will agree.
By the terms of the British North America Act, set out in section No. 91, this parliament has exclusive authority to raise money by any

The Budget-Mr. Small mode or system of taxation. It also sets out in section No. 92 that each province has the exclusive right to raise revenue by direct taxes for provincial purposes. To this everyone is in agreement-as to the power of both bodies being able to collect by direct taxes.
The difference arises out of who will have priority in collecting, or who will carry the opprobrium of being the body making the second collection when agreement cannot be effected to collect by a single collection. Notwithstanding what has been said by the Minister of Finance, and his examples of how in some of the states in the United States they have dual taxes, there is this difference: Whether it was done by tacit agreement or understanding, the provinces were the only bodies employing direct taxation from confederation up to the year 1917, when the then finance minister, the Hon. Thomas White, under the stress and demand for more revenue to carry on world war I, introduced the first dominion income tax, and went into considerable explanation for so doing, and why they had to invade what was recognized by all as the exclusive taxing field of the provinces.
This remained the situation up to world war II, with parliament utilizing only one of the fields of direct taxes, but during the interval from confederation to world war II some provinces had intermittently used the personal income tax for revenue.
With the heavy demand during the dark days of world war II, to obtain further revenue parliament then made a proposition to the provinces to invade the fields of succession duties, corporation, transportation and amusement taxes, and the provinces, motivated by patriotism, did, by a fiscal agreement, vacate their taxing fields for the duration of the war, actually renting them to parliament, after which, unless further agreements were made, a return to the status quo would ensue.
The situation now prevailing is that the government has made separate agreements with every province except one, instead of by the original method of a dominion-provincial conference when a general agreement was amicably worked out. The government has manoeuvred itself into the position that it is reluctant to give up and return to the status quo, to which they originally agreed.
Now then, if the government did not believe that the provinces had some claim through their long tenure of occupancy from confederation, notwithstanding the government's constitutional position, why did they enter into these tax rental agreements with the provinces to vacate their taxing fields? The only conclusion we can arrive at is that


they had to jockey into a position where they had possession and be in complete control, to be the first to levy taxes, and a province or provinces which did not enter into an agreement with them would have to bear the full odium of having imposed a double tax when the real offender is the government, by virtue of the facts and conditions I have outlined.
This is a matter of grave concern, not only to one province but to all provinces, and some consideration should be given to the provinces because of their vested rights in the long uninterrupted occupancy of their taxing fields.
It is unfortunate that the impact had to come upon the government from the province whence they get their greatest support. The government is now caught in the milieu of their hybrid Chauvinism. This Liberal party has been so long in office by reason of its hold on Quebec. It held Quebec by a deliberate policy of banking the fires of racial prejudice. Now these fires are bursting into flames, and severely scorching the faces of the federal Liberals.
We Conservatives live and think in the tradition of Sir John A. Macdonald. It was he who saw the vision of a united Canada- French and English-neither one of the two main racial origins seeking votes by trying to exploit its unnatural prejudices, but living and working together in mutual self-respect for the common weal of the nation.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I waited until now to take part in the present debate on the budget, it is because, faced with the confusion which seems to exist and with the complexity of the problem created by the unilateral decision of the Quebec government to collect a personal income tax-the move being based on the alleged priority of the legislature in respect to direct taxation-I felt under the obligation to listen first of all to the representations of the electors of the riding I have the honour of representing here as well as to the various arguments which would be put forward, before taking a definite stand.
It was my duty to take such an attitude because the problem has assumed new aspects and can give rise to grave consequences, in the provinces as well as in the entire country. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) said here that much too bitter terms had been used since the government of my province announced that it would collect a personal income tax equal to 15 per cent, inasmuch as it was free to refuse to participate in

the fiscal agreements, freely signed by the other provinces in co-operation with the Canadian government, and as certain nonpolitical organizations have asked the latter that permission be given to deduct the provincial tax from the federal tax.
I am taking for granted and I recognize, following the statement made this afternoon by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent, that the government of the province of Quebec did not itself ask for this deductibility and that no official approach has yet been attempted by the Quebec government in order to obtain this deductibility of 15 per cent, if press conferences, that are often characterized by considerations of party politics, have not admittedly become the consecrated formula for an exchange of views between the various governments of this country. As the newspaper Le Devoir, which is not lacking in ideas, says, it would be introducing a "new look", a twentieth century look, in federal-provincial relations.
As during the time allotted to me, 1 intend to speak about federal-provincial relations from the point of view of fiscal authority, I hope to be pardoned if I hesitate to utter my remarks in the manner of our opponents, in whose speeches the confusion raised by their ideas is only equalled by the contradictory spirit pervading all their policy announcements, according to the time or place of their statements.
The Conservative member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) contradicted the hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Dufresne) when he said, on April 28, as reported at page 4211 of Hansard, that the agreements concluded between the Canadian government on the one hand, and the provincial legislatures on the other are legal, while the hon. member for Quebec West had stated emphatically, on April 27 of this year, as reported at page 4159 of Hansard, that the fiscal agreements were illegal. And then the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer) told us, on behalf of the party to which he belongs, that the Conservative party recognizes and supports the principle of deductibility which was accepted following a resolution of the general convention of the Conservative party. The official financial critic of the Conservative party (Mr. Macdonnell) and his leader himself, in an accusing silence, are not even bold enough to refer to that doctrine in the present debate, leaving us under the impression that they do not support the stand taken by their senior member from Quebec.
The only spirit which now moves me is a feeling that I share with a large number of my fellow citizens. We are worried about
The Budget-Mr. Maltais the 300,000 Quebec taxpayers who will have to bear the burden of double taxation, and the lack of understanding which still remains in the minds of some of them who still do not understand the failure of their government to accept the 15 per cent deduction formula put forward, which would allow the Quebec government to obtain an amount lower than that which it would have received had it entered into an agreement.
I stated a moment ago that the situation resulting from the unilateral decision of the government of my province of levying a tax on personal income and then trying through subrogation, that is through the help of nonpolitical organizations, to obtain deduction of that tax, without previous agreement to that effect, gave rise to a very complicated problem owing to the fiscal agreements binding the federal government and nine other provinces.
In my humble opinion, the solution to that problem, owing to its constitutional implications, its social and economic consequences as well as its political impact, must take all those factors into consideration. I think that a proposed agreement that would not take these various elements into consideration might well remain inoperative. I shall go even further and state that a long-term and permanent solution must also take into account the special position of the province of Quebec because of the distinctive character of the racial group that makes up its population.
I was happy the other day to hear once again the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Breton) assert that the Liberal party was, of all political parties, the one truly Canadian and national party, the one that had best understood the position of Quebec. I am confident that the Liberal party which now presides over the destinies of the nation, will be able to find the remedy to those growing pains which have now developed between the government of my province and that of my country in the taxation field.
In speaking thus, Mr. Speaker, I do not want to shirk my responsibilities by refraining from making the remarks I proposed to make about that stalemate or, at the risk of repeating myself, about those growing pains of the Canadian nation.
I would like first of all to speak about the constitutional aspect of the matter, of its social character, and then of its economic and political implications.
In the constitutional sphere, most glaring contradictions have been expressed. It has been said that provincial legislatures had exclusive

The Budget-Mr. Maltais jurisdiction in the field of direct taxation, as has been asserted this afternoon by the hon. member for Chicoutimi (Mr. Gagnon), who later said that this right was prior to that of central government. As far as I am concerned, I share the opinion of those who believe that the rights of the Canadian government in matters of direct taxation are equal to and concurrent with the rights of the provinces and that there is no prior right, neither in favour of the central government nor in favour of a provincial government.
The British North America Act of 1867 embodied that principle under section 91 which grants the Canadian government the power to raise money by any mode or system of taxation, and under section 92 which grants the provincial legislature the power to raise money by means of direct taxation within the province for provincial purposes.
That, Mr. Speaker, is what the Canadian constitution provides, and though I am not a lawyer, I can hardly see how this text could be read as granting a prior right to either one of the two authorities. It is true that the word "exclusively" appears in the preamble of section 92, but the same word is to be found also in the preamble of section 91. On the other hand, it is not the first time the Canadian government holds powers concurrent with those of the provincial legislatures.
Many more examples could be quoted in the sphere of Canadian political activities where the jurisdiction of the central government runs parallel with the jurisdiction of the various legislatures.
Is that not, in any event, the very point which has been an issue between the federal government and the provincial governments since the early days of confederation? That point of view will be readily understood if only we remind ourselves of the thousands of dollars which the Canadian people have had to pay in legal costs while endeavouring to obtain a determination of certain rights or a clear definition of the meaning of certain sections of our Canadian constitution.
How is it that no authority has ever tried to bring before the courts this matter of concurrent and equal jurisdiction in the matter of direct taxation, since this state of affairs has existed since 1917? Along with the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Lesage) I would say that that alone proves that the theory of priority rights in the matter of direct taxation is something new and would be extremely difficult to prove. I am not sure, though, that the privy council did not hand down a decision in that connection, in London, around 1936.

The hon. members of this house will no doubt recall that Manitoba citizen who challenged the right of his province to impose an income tax, under the pretext that income could not be taxed twice, namely by the federal government and the provincial government at the same time. I now refer to the judgment of the privy council in the case of Forbes v. the Attorney General, where the following may be found, at page 260:
Both income taxes (federal and provincial) may co-exist and be enforced without conflict. The federal government taxes part of the Manitoba citizen's income, the province taxes the other part.
That judgment speaks for itself. In addition, the question of the levying of taxes and that of their distribution is intimately connected, according to the spirit and the interpretation of confederation.
Without going into the merits of subsidies, I must just the same admit that it is fair and honest to look for an interpretation of the Canadian constitution with the fathers of confederation themselves, who, in addition to giving us our constitution, also put it to the test during the few years following 1867. What was, then, the fiscal policy in 1868 and during the ensuing years?
In 1868, on the morrow of the birth of the Canadian constitution, the province of Quebec received from Ottawa, by way of subsidy, the amount of $913,412, or 59-7 per cent of the total budget of the province. In 1869, the Quebec budget was made up to the extent of 59-2 per cent of Ottawa subsidies, in 1870, of 52 per cent, in 1871 of 49 per cent, and in 1872, that is five years after the passing of the confederation act, the budget of the province of Quebec consisted of subsidies from Ottawa to the extent of 47-1 per cent.
These, Mr. Speaker, are true facts in the constitutional field that nobody is able to deny and that prove without ambiguity, that in 1954, the matter of subsidies, even if related to a power of taxation belonging to the provinces, may not be quoted in this debate as an argument contrary to the spirit of confederation. The hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Girard) tried to argue, with the help of quotations from the fathers of confederation, that the spirit of the British North America Act was contrary to the policy of subsidies resulting from fiscal agreements. He quoted Brown in support of his argument.
To paraphrase the saying of a French author, I might tell him: Give me something taken out of its context and I can succeed in having the author of the words hanged. He found that a quotation of Brown's declara-

tions could be of use to him. I shall therefore go to that same Mr. Brown for a statement which will contradict him. I borrow a quotation from the official report of the debates preceding confederation, page 93, where Mr. Brown was dealing with the question of federal subsidies:
We had to face the following alternative: grant to the provinces the revenue from indirect taxation, which field we wanted to leave exclusively to the central government, or allow the central authority the right to collect the money and allocate it afterwards to the various local governments to enable them to face their local needs. We chose the latter solution.
If words have any meaning, that statement of a father of confederation is abso-
The Budget-Mr. Maltais lutely different from the impression which my hon. friend from Lapointe tried to give in quoting this great Canadian.
